items.summary_html:
How LLMs remember context without recomputing everything
TL;DR
Generating each new token requires attention over every previous token. Without caching, the model would redo that work on every single step.
The keys and values of past tokens never change, so they are computed once and stored. That store is the KV cache.
Its size is fixed per token by the model’s architecture, and it scales with context length × concurrent users. It routinely exceeds the size of the model weights.
Reserving memory per sequence up front wastes most of it, because you never know how long a response will be.
PagedAttention stores the cache in small fixed-size blocks instead, allocated on demand — which is where a large share of modern serving throughput comes from.
When the pool fills, the engine evicts running requests. Cache memory is what actually caps concurrency.

Ask an LLM a question and the answer arrives one token at a time. To produce each token, the model attends to everything before it — the prompt and every token it has already generated.

Done naively, that is a staggering amount of repeated work. Generating token 500 would mean reprocessing 499 tokens that were already processed to generate token 499, which had already reprocessed the 498 before it.

The KV cache is what stops that. It is a simple idea with outsized consequences: it is usually the largest dynamic consumer of GPU memory in a serving system, and it — not compute — is what decides how many users a GPU can hold.

This article covers what it stores, what it costs, how it is managed, and what happens when it runs out.

1. What attention needs

A short primer, only as much as we need.

For every token it processes, a transformer produces three vectors:

Query (Q) — what this token is looking for. Key (K) — what this token offers, so other tokens can find it. Value (V) — the actual information this token contributes.

To compute the output for a given token, the model compares that token’s query against the keys of all preceding tokens, and uses the resulting weights to blend their values.

So generating a new token requires the K and V of every token before it.

2. The observation that makes caching possible

Here is the property everything depends on.

When the model generates token 501, it needs the keys and values of tokens 1 through 500. Those keys and values were already computed when those tokens were processed — and they do not change. Token 200’s key is a function of token 200 and the tokens before it. Adding new tokens to the end of the sequence does not alter it.

The queries are different: each new token needs a fresh query. But queries are needed only for the token being generated right now, and then discarded.

Generating a new token needs:

  Q  →  only for the current token   →  compute fresh, throw away
  K  →  for every previous token     →  same as last step
  V  →  for every previous token     →  same as last step

So the keys and values get computed once and kept. That store is the KV cache.

Without it, every generation step reprocesses the entire context. With it, each step processes exactly one new token and reads the rest from memory.

3. What it costs

The cache is not free, and its size is fixed by the model’s architecture. Per token:

bytes per token = 2 × layers × KV heads × head dimension × bytes per value

The leading 2 is for K and V. Every layer keeps its own, because attention happens at every layer.

For a 70B-class model with 80 layers, 8 KV heads, a head dimension of 128, in 16-bit precision:

2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes ≈ 320 KB per token

That looks small. Now scale it:

8,000 tokens of context  ≈   2.5 GB   for one user
   100 users at 8,000 tokens  ≈   250 GB

Compare that with the model itself, which needs roughly 140 GB of weights at the same precision. The cache for a hundred moderately-long conversations is larger than the model.

This is the fact that surprises people. Weights are the number everyone sizes hardware on, and in a busy deployment they are frequently the smaller half of the memory budget.

4. Two axes, not one

The cache grows along two dimensions at once, and both are outside your control.

Context length. Every token added to a conversation adds its slice. A conversation that has been running for a while costs more than a fresh one, even from the same user.

Concurrency. Every simultaneous request has its own cache. They do not share anything.

Multiply them and you get the real number. This is why a deployment can be perfectly stable at a hundred short conversations and fall over at twenty long ones, on identical hardware with identical compute.

It also means capacity questions are unanswerable in the abstract. “How many users can this GPU serve?” has no answer without a context length attached to it.

5. The allocation problem

So we know what to store. The harder question is where — and this is where naive implementations lose most of their memory.

The difficulty: you do not know how long a sequence will be. A request arrives with a 200-token prompt. Will the answer be 5 tokens or 5,000? Nobody knows, including the model.

Early serving systems handled this by reserving a contiguous region large enough for the maximum supported length, for every sequence. If the model supports 32,000 tokens, every request reserves 32,000 tokens’ worth of cache the moment it is admitted.

The waste is severe, and it comes in three forms:

Over-reservation. A request that generates 100 tokens holds a 32,000-token reservation for its entire life. Over 99% of that memory is untouched but unavailable to anyone else.

Internal fragmentation. Even when a sequence does grow, the unused tail of its reservation sits idle until it gets there — which it may never do.

External fragmentation. Requests finish in a different order than they started, leaving gaps of free memory between live reservations. The gaps may add up to plenty of space, but if none is large enough to hold a new contiguous reservation, a new request cannot be admitted.

The vLLM paper that introduced PagedAttention reported that systems of this kind wasted the large majority of their KV cache memory. Which meant the practical limit on concurrency was not the hardware — it was the allocator.

6. PagedAttention: stop reserving, start allocating

The fix is to abandon the requirement that a sequence’s cache be contiguous.

PagedAttention splits the cache into small fixed-size blocks, each holding a fixed number of tokens (16 is a common default). A sequence is allocated blocks as it grows, one at a time, and those blocks can sit anywhere in the pool. A per-sequence block table records which physical blocks hold which part of the sequence, and the attention kernel follows that table when it reads.

PagedAttention Memory

The technique is borrowed from operating system virtual memory, which is where the name comes from — pages, page tables, and a layer of indirection between logical and physical addresses.

Three things change immediately:

No over-reservation. A sequence holds only the blocks it has actually filled. A 100-token answer uses seven blocks, not two thousand.

No external fragmentation. Every block is the same size, so any free block fits any sequence. Free memory is never unusable because of its shape.

Waste is bounded. The only unused space is the partially-filled last block of each sequence — at most 15 tokens’ worth. Compared to reserving thousands, this is nothing.

The practical effect is that far more sequences fit in the same VRAM. Since concurrency is what drives batching, and batching is what drives throughput, better cache allocation translates fairly directly into more tokens per second from the same GPU.

7. When the pool fills up

Blocks are allocated on demand, which raises an obvious question: what happens when a running sequence needs a new block and none is free?

The engine has to take memory from someone. It preempts a running request, freeing its blocks, and resumes it later when space is available. Two ways to do that:

Recompute. Discard the sequence’s cache entirely. When it resumes, run prefill again over its tokens to rebuild the state. Cheap to evict, expensive to restore.

Swap. Copy the blocks out to CPU memory and copy them back on resume. Preserves the work, but pays the cost of moving data across the PCIe link in both directions.

Either way, from the user’s side this appears as a response that stalls mid-generation and then continues. From the operator’s side, frequent preemption is a clear signal that the deployment is running past its memory limits — usually the point to reduce concurrency, shorten the maximum context, or add capacity.

This is also the mechanism behind a claim that sounds odd until you know where it comes from: concurrency in an LLM server is capped by cache memory, not by compute. The GPU is rarely out of arithmetic. It is out of blocks.

8. Making the cache smaller

Since cache size is set by architecture and context, there are only a few levers.

Grouped-query attention (GQA) is the big one, and it is why the number in Section 3 was as small as it was. In classic multi-head attention, every attention head keeps its own K and V. GQA has several query heads share one set, cutting the KV heads dramatically. That 70B example used 8 KV heads; with 64 it would have been eight times larger — 2.5 MB per token instead of 320 KB. Nearly every recent model uses GQA or a variant, and it is largely a serving-cost decision.

KV cache quantization stores keys and values in 8-bit instead of 16-bit, halving the cache at some cost to quality. Independent of weight quantization — you can do either, or both.

Context limits. Capping the maximum accepted context bounds what any single request can consume, protecting everyone else’s capacity. Blunt, but effective and entirely under your control.

Longer-term architectural work — sliding-window attention, sparse and linear attention, cross-layer sharing — aims at changing the growth curve rather than its constant. This is an active area and worth watching if long context matters to your workload.

9. The mental model

Four sentences hold most of it:

The weights are static, shared by everyone, and sized once. The KV cache is dynamic, private to each request, and grows with both context length and concurrency. Whatever VRAM the weights do not occupy becomes the cache pool. How efficiently that pool is managed determines how many users the GPU can serve.

That is why memory management is not a detail of LLM serving. It is most of it.

The next problem

There is one thing we have quietly accepted throughout.

When a request finishes, its cache is released. The blocks return to the pool and their contents are gone. That is correct — the conversation is over, the state is not needed.

But look at what actually flows through a production deployment. Every request from the same application begins with the same system prompt, often thousands of tokens of instructions and policy. Every follow-up turn in a chat re-sends the entire conversation so far. Users in the same product ask questions against the same documents.

The prefixes are identical. And we compute them from scratch, every single time, throwing the result away at the end of each request.

That is a lot of work being repeated — the very thing the KV cache was invented to avoid, reappearing one level up. Within a request we already refuse to recompute. Across requests, we do nothing.

If two requests start with the same tokens, why compute the same cache twice?

That question turns out to have a genuinely interesting answer.

items.title: I left Texas for Europe more than a decade ago. Living in France is affordable, and I'm happier.
items.summary: Leah Young at the Eiffel Tower. Courtesy of Leah Young Leah Young moved from Texas to Spain in 2015 and now lives in Lyon, France. Young says she's happy with her life in France, which includes access to affordable, high-quality healthcare. Her one-bedroom apartment costs her $1,104 each month, and she spends $70 a week on food. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Leah Young, a 34-year-old from Dallas who moved to Spain in 2015. Young is the founder of Fearless Abroad , a company that helps Americans working remotely relocate to Europe. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity. A lot of people love the idea of traveling to new places and experiencing something exciting. What excited me about living abroad was the adventure. When I was younger, I'd taken a few short trips, but there was still so much more of the world I wanted to see. For years, I tried to make it happen. In high school and college, I looked into exchange programs and studying abroad, but my family was always like, "No way." Eventually, a friend mentioned a government-run teaching program in Spain that had an open call for applications. I jumped at it, even though I was working in a completely different industry. I figured it was finally a way to get to Europe . I thought I'd spend just one year abroad, then return to Texas and live my life as I always had. But that year turned into many, and I stayed, though in different ways over time. I was terrified to move to Europe Preparing to leave for Europe was really scary. I had never lived abroad, and I didn't know anyone else who had. I remember thinking, "How practical is this, really?" The visa process was stressful. My teaching program gave me permission to come, but I still had to handle the visa process myself. I got through it by diving deep into Facebook groups and random blogs, piecing everything together and learning as much as I could. I was really worried about whether I could afford the cost of living in Spain. Yes, I was moving with a job contract, but I would earn only €700 ($813) a month. Even in 2015, that wasn't much. I didn't know whether it would cover my rent, let alone leave money for anything else. There were so many other things I had to figure out, like whether to cancel my US health insurance — my government contract came with Spanish coverage — and what to do with my phone plan, car, dishes, furniture, and everything else in my apartment. In the end, I left the US with nothing but two suitcases, filled with all the wrong things, and a visa. The truth is, I was totally freaked out. But I went for it because I saw that other people had made it work — and, ultimately, I did, too. Lyon was the perfect place for me I feel like I've become an expert at starting over. After living in Spain for five years, I spent two years in Germany, a year in Argentina, a year in Brazil, and now I've been in France for a year. I live in Lyon, about two hours from Geneva, near the Swiss border. It's very close to the mountains, so within an hour or two, you can be skiing in the Alps, or you could be swimming in the Mediterranean Sea. Lyon, France. Gary Yeowell/Getty Images Lyon is quintessentially what you'd imagine traditional France to be. It's a really nice second option to living in Paris . While it's a large city, it has a small-town feel. I've traveled and lived around Europe, and in some places, I found people a little closed off or hard to build relationships with. That was a real struggle for me because, as a Texan, I'm outgoing and want to make friends and build a community. But since moving here, I've found it much easier to make friends. My life feels pretty affordable Finding a place to live in Lyon can be competitive, but I got really lucky. I found my apartment within two days through word of mouth. I was chatting with someone who knew a person with an available apartment, and that's how I got it. I pay €950 ($1,104) a month in rent for a beautiful 678-square-foot one-bedroom apartment in a historic building dating back to the 1500s. It has fantastic stone walls, tall ceilings with wooden beams, and massive French windows overlooking the old town. I can even hear the clock tower ring every half hour. Young at Lyon Cathedral. Courtesy of Leah Young My utility bill varies a lot. It's pretty affordable in the summer, since I don't use air conditioning, and I might pay only €50 ($58) a month. But winters can be expensive because it gets chilly, and I live in an old building. During the coldest months, my heating bill can be around €350 ($407). Overall, I'd say living in Lyon is pretty affordable. I cook a lot and spend about €60 ($70) a week on groceries. I usually eat out only twice a week, and getting a glass of wine or a beer might cost €5 ($6). I also don't have a car, nor do I need one. I spend less than $10 a week getting around on the train. Taking trips can be really cheap, too. It might cost me around €50 ($58) round trip to fly to Germany. I don't think I'll ever move back to the US I've had a lot of different jobs during my time abroad. When I first arrived, I was teaching. Then I switched to a student visa and went back to school. For a while, I worked remotely for a US-based company. Now, I own a business that helps other remote workers relocate to Europe . Even so, I've visited my family in the US many times over the years and considered moving back, but it just hasn't worked for me. It's so expensive, especially in Texas, where things are booming , and rents have gotten crazy. It always blows me away to see people paying $2,000 a month for a one-bedroom apartment. Healthcare is another reason Europe suits me better. The quality is great, but it doesn't feel like it costs a million dollars, as it does in the US. That feels especially valuable as I get older and think about having kids. Young at a restaurant. Courtesy of Leah Young Of course, there are things I miss about the US, like my family and friends. I miss the ease of conversation, too — being able to crack a joke without worrying that it'll be misunderstood. And honestly, I miss the food, especially steak and Tex-Mex . Texas has the best food in the world, if you ask me. I do think France is my permanent home , but it's hard to say for sure. Can anyone really tell you where they'll be in 10 years? Of all the moves I've made, though, I'm happiest here. It feels like home, and I'm at a point in my life where I'm ready to settle down. Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
Leah Young at the Eiffel Tower.

Courtesy of Leah Young

  • Leah Young moved from Texas to Spain in 2015 and now lives in Lyon, France.
  • Young says she's happy with her life in France, which includes access to affordable, high-quality healthcare.
  • Her one-bedroom apartment costs her $1,104 each month, and she spends $70 a week on food.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Leah Young, a 34-year-old from Dallas who moved to Spain in 2015. Young is the founder of Fearless Abroad, a company that helps Americans working remotely relocate to Europe. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

A lot of people love the idea of traveling to new places and experiencing something exciting. What excited me about living abroad was the adventure. When I was younger, I'd taken a few short trips, but there was still so much more of the world I wanted to see.

For years, I tried to make it happen. In high school and college, I looked into exchange programs and studying abroad, but my family was always like, "No way."

Eventually, a friend mentioned a government-run teaching program in Spain that had an open call for applications. I jumped at it, even though I was working in a completely different industry. I figured it was finally a way to get to Europe.

I thought I'd spend just one year abroad, then return to Texas and live my life as I always had. But that year turned into many, and I stayed, though in different ways over time.

I was terrified to move to Europe

Preparing to leave for Europe was really scary. I had never lived abroad, and I didn't know anyone else who had. I remember thinking, "How practical is this, really?"

The visa process was stressful. My teaching program gave me permission to come, but I still had to handle the visa process myself. I got through it by diving deep into Facebook groups and random blogs, piecing everything together and learning as much as I could.

I was really worried about whether I could afford the cost of living in Spain. Yes, I was moving with a job contract, but I would earn only €700 ($813) a month. Even in 2015, that wasn't much. I didn't know whether it would cover my rent, let alone leave money for anything else.

There were so many other things I had to figure out, like whether to cancel my US health insurance — my government contract came with Spanish coverage — and what to do with my phone plan, car, dishes, furniture, and everything else in my apartment.

In the end, I left the US with nothing but two suitcases, filled with all the wrong things, and a visa. The truth is, I was totally freaked out. But I went for it because I saw that other people had made it work — and, ultimately, I did, too.

Lyon was the perfect place for me

I feel like I've become an expert at starting over. After living in Spain for five years, I spent two years in Germany, a year in Argentina, a year in Brazil, and now I've been in France for a year.

I live in Lyon, about two hours from Geneva, near the Swiss border. It's very close to the mountains, so within an hour or two, you can be skiing in the Alps, or you could be swimming in the Mediterranean Sea.

Lyon, France.

Gary Yeowell/Getty Images

Lyon is quintessentially what you'd imagine traditional France to be. It's a really nice second option to living in Paris. While it's a large city, it has a small-town feel.

I've traveled and lived around Europe, and in some places, I found people a little closed off or hard to build relationships with. That was a real struggle for me because, as a Texan, I'm outgoing and want to make friends and build a community. But since moving here, I've found it much easier to make friends.

My life feels pretty affordable

Finding a place to live in Lyon can be competitive, but I got really lucky. I found my apartment within two days through word of mouth. I was chatting with someone who knew a person with an available apartment, and that's how I got it.

I pay €950 ($1,104) a month in rent for a beautiful 678-square-foot one-bedroom apartment in a historic building dating back to the 1500s. It has fantastic stone walls, tall ceilings with wooden beams, and massive French windows overlooking the old town. I can even hear the clock tower ring every half hour.

Young at Lyon Cathedral.

Courtesy of Leah Young

My utility bill varies a lot. It's pretty affordable in the summer, since I don't use air conditioning, and I might pay only €50 ($58) a month. But winters can be expensive because it gets chilly, and I live in an old building. During the coldest months, my heating bill can be around €350 ($407).

Overall, I'd say living in Lyon is pretty affordable. I cook a lot and spend about €60 ($70) a week on groceries. I usually eat out only twice a week, and getting a glass of wine or a beer might cost €5 ($6). I also don't have a car, nor do I need one. I spend less than $10 a week getting around on the train. Taking trips can be really cheap, too. It might cost me around €50 ($58) round trip to fly to Germany.

I don't think I'll ever move back to the US

I've had a lot of different jobs during my time abroad. When I first arrived, I was teaching. Then I switched to a student visa and went back to school. For a while, I worked remotely for a US-based company. Now, I own a business that helps other remote workers relocate to Europe.

Even so, I've visited my family in the US many times over the years and considered moving back, but it just hasn't worked for me.

It's so expensive, especially in Texas, where things are booming, and rents have gotten crazy. It always blows me away to see people paying $2,000 a month for a one-bedroom apartment.

Healthcare is another reason Europe suits me better. The quality is great, but it doesn't feel like it costs a million dollars, as it does in the US. That feels especially valuable as I get older and think about having kids.

Young at a restaurant.

Courtesy of Leah Young

Of course, there are things I miss about the US, like my family and friends. I miss the ease of conversation, too — being able to crack a joke without worrying that it'll be misunderstood. And honestly, I miss the food, especially steak and Tex-Mex. Texas has the best food in the world, if you ask me.

I do think France is my permanent home, but it's hard to say for sure. Can anyone really tell you where they'll be in 10 years? Of all the moves I've made, though, I'm happiest here. It feels like home, and I'm at a point in my life where I'm ready to settle down.

The first teaser for the resulting documentary, "You Can See Everything," makes it seem like a mind-bending thriller starring the fallen tech visionary.

A24 surprised critics at the Telluride Film Festival on Sunday night with a screening of the closely held project, which had been kept under wraps for three years. It hits theaters in October.

Journalists who attended the screening wrote that phones and smart glasses were bagged upon entry. The festival director asked for secrecy on plot twists and a celebrity cameo.

"What happens in Telluride stays in Telluride," she told the crowd, Los Angeles Times reporter Josh Rottenberg recalled.

— A24 (@A24) September 7, 2026

Comic Nathan Fielder and filmmaker Lance Oppenheim, whose A24 feature "Primetime" is also making the festival circuit, directed the documentary. Fielder's signature blurring of real life and character acting is on full display as he presses Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, on whether they are telling him the truth.

A one-minute teaser shows an exchange between Holmes and Fielder. Holmes insists she has nothing to hide.

"I'm not that person," she says, adding that she is engaging with him "as a human being." Fielder then asks whether she is being real.

"I'm always being real," Holmes responds, unblinking.

Elizabeth Holmes, center, arrives at Federal Prison Camp Bryan in Bryan, Texas, on May 30, 2023.

At 19, Holmes set out to build a diagnostics company that could run a battery of blood tests with a few drops of blood. Then came a Wall Street Journal inquiry that exposed serious problems with the Theranos technology, setting off the company's unraveling.

Holmes was sentenced to 11 years in prison after being found guilty on four counts that included fraud and conspiracy. Her projected release date is in 2031.

items.title: OpenAI’s new model costs 2.5x more per token — and developers are saving money anyway
items.summary: GPT-6 Astra has an obvious problem for developers considering an upgrade from GPT-5.6 Sol: its tokens cost 2.5 times as much, yet OpenAI thinks many developers should upgrade anyway — and then turn the reasoning setting down. OpenAI’s Thibault Sottiaux , engineering lead for Codex, posted on X over the weekend saying, “To calibrate you all on which reasoning effort to use for Astra, know that GPT-6 Astra on low performs better than GPT-5.6 Sol on high.” Artificial Analysis currently scores Astra-low at 49 on its Intelligence Index, narrowly ahead of Sol-high at 48 . Astra-low also responded much sooner, with the first token arriving in 2.53 seconds, compared to 11.87 seconds for Sol-high. “To calibrate you all on which reasoning effort to use for Astra, know that GPT-6 Astra on low performs better than GPT-5.6 Sol on high.” Reasoning effort changes cost Astra costs $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens , compared with $4 and $20 for Sol at current rates. Moving the reasoning dial from high to low doesn’t change those rates, but it can change how much work gets done before the task is finally complete and it’s an argument OpenAI makes explicitly in its migration guidance. The company says Astra can produce stronger results while using substantially fewer output tokens. OpenAI uses its own benchmark as proof. The company saw the same pattern in Terminal-Bench 4.0 , where Astra scored 57.9% to Sol’s 37.3% but still cost about 9% less per task. The gap was even wider on GPQA Diamond: Astra edged out Sol, 94.9% to 94.6%, at an estimated cost 37% lower. Real-world workloads will vary, but the results suggest that per-token pricing alone does not tell developers what a model will actually cost to run — an idea OpenAI is already exploring with outcome-based pricing . Fewer tokens, cheaper tasks Developer Shinpr ran the comparison on the same codebase, using Sol-high and several Astra reasoning levels, with analysis, implementation, and review. Astra-medium did better on both time and cost by handling the implementation in 80 requests, less than a third of the 238 Sol-high needed, and processed 11.1 million input tokens instead of 37.8 million. By the end of all three phases, the Astra-medium run had taken about 51 minutes and cost an estimated $25.67; the Sol-high run had taken roughly 75 minutes and cost $31.79. Turning Astra up to high didn’t help because that run stretched to 77 minutes and $37.23, and Shinpr said its review missed a startup bug that medium caught. One developer’s test can’t tell us that medium will be the right choice for every workload, but it does indicate that more reasoning wasn’t worth paying for here. Also, that pattern doesn’t hold everywhere. ARC Prize’s testing went in almost the opposite direction. Turning Astra up to high didn’t help because that run stretched to 77 minutes and $37.23, and Shinpr said its review missed a startup bug that medium caught. More reasoning, lower bills ARC Prize’s evaluation of Astra shows the other side of the equation. More reasoning not only improved Astra’s score on ARC-AGI-3; in some cases, it also reduced costs. With ARC Prize’s standard harness, Astra scored 17.5% at low reasoning, 38.6% at medium, 54.8% at high, and 62.7% at max. Astra also has an xhigh setting between high and max . But the most expensive runs weren’t the ones using the most reasoning. ARC Prize spent $38,166 at low, $48,090 at medium, and $40,705 at high. Max came in at just $26,098. At max, Astra used more compute on each decision but needed fewer actions to solve the environments. That tradeoff was enough to bring the overall cost down, which can happen with agents. While lower reasoning may look cheaper, a wrong turn quickly means another tool call or another attempt after another, which costs more in reasoning upfront than just fixing the mistakes later. While lower reasoning may look cheaper, a wrong turn quickly means another tool call or another attempt after another, which costs more in reasoning upfront than just fixing the mistakes later. Dynamic reasoning without cache loss Those are two extremes that developers don’t need to choose between for their entire workflow, thanks to Astra introducing a configuration_update mechanism that lets an application change the reasoning effort between responses without changing the original request-level configuration. Routine work can remain at a low reasoning level, while a failed test, an unexpected tool response, or a difficult debugging problem can trigger a higher reasoning level for the next turn. Once that’s resolved, the agent can drop back down. That also helps explain why Shinpr and ARC Prize got such different results. Shinpr found that extra reasoning added time and cost without improving the outcome, while ARC Prize found that more reasoning sometimes cut the number of actions enough to lower the total bill. For now, configuration_update only works with Astra in standard, single-agent requests. But, don’t get hung up on Astra’s 2.5x token price. An expensive model is often the cheaper run if it takes fewer calls to finish the job and fewer attempts to get it right. items.title: I Benchmarked Every MTP Depth on Qwen3.8–27B-UD-Q4. Here You Are.
items.summary: I Benchmarked Every MTP Depth on Qwen3.8–27B-UD-Q4_K_M/XL. Here You Are. Normal decoding is one forward pass per-token. That is the entire bottleneck of local inference. TL;DR MTP on Qwen3.8–27B-UD-Q4 gives a genuine ~2× on a 4090: 48.5 → 96.2 t/s on K_M, 46.3 → 84.2 t/s on K_XL. The useful band for draft_num_predict is 2 to 5, and 5 is the pick: best on K_M, best on K_XL, best average, best worst case. Above 5 both builds lose ground. Drafting more tokens does not raise how many get accepted per verification pass, so the extra drafts are pure cost. Above 8 on K_XL, or 11 on K_M, you are actively destroying performance (up to 5.3× slower than not using MTP at all). Those two numbers are three apart, on the same model and the same card, and that is the whole reason “use a low value” was never a sufficient answer . The heavier quant breaks earlier. Your card will break somewhere else. Seventeen Gigabytes of Weights Moved to Produce a Single Token (By Author, Powered by Gemini) At 27B parameters and 4-bit weights on my RTX 4090, one decode step costs roughly 20.6 ms and produces exactly one token. That is where my ~48 tokens/s comes from, and no amount of clever prompting changes it. The trick behind speculative decoding is that the forward pass is bound by memory bandwidth, not by compute. You are dragging seventeen gigabytes of weights across the memory bus to produce a single token. If you happened to have several candidate tokens sitting there, you could verify all of them in that same pass for nearly no extra cost, because the weights are already in flight. Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) is where those candidates come from. unsloth/Qwen3.8–27B-GGUF ships with a small head trained to guess the next few tokens. The head drafts, the full model verifies. Every draft that matches what the model would have produced anyway is a free token. Every draft that doesn’t is thrown away, and you fall back to the one token you were going to get regardless. Two things follow, and both matter for the rest of this article. First, MTP is not a quality tradeoff. The verification step is what makes it safe: a drafted token only survives if the main model agrees with it. NVIDIA’s primer on the technique puts it plainly: when the draft is wrong, the target model just decodes normally, so the output is not degraded . This is not quantization. You are not trading precision for speed. You are trading VRAM for speed. Second, it is not free. The draft head has to live in memory, the drafted tokens have to be generated, and the verification pass has to chew through all of them whether they are accepted or not. On the Unsloth model card, the MTP module for Qwen3.8–27B ships as a single Q4_0 file of about 1.37 GB (no separate MTP build per quantization). You download the same module whether you run UD-Q4_K_M, UD-Q4_K_XL or anything else, and it costs the same gigabyte and change either way. On a 24 GB card, 1.37 GB is not pocket money. That is the whole tension. 1. The problem: everybody says “low,” nobody says how low draft_num_predict N is the knob. It tells the runtime how many tokens to draft per verification pass. N=0 turns MTP off. When I went looking for a starting value, every source agreed on the shape of the advice (keep it small, more is not better) and disagreed on the number. Recommended Draft Depth by Source, and the Range They Span (By Author) One, two, three, five, six. All of them are “low.” All of them come from people who know exactly what they are doing. The spread between smallest and largest is a factor of six, and every one of those pages tells you, correctly, that the right answer depends on your hardware. Unsloth is the most explicit: try 1 through 6, keep whichever is fastest, and do not assume their starting number is optimal because performance is hardware-dependent . Honest advice, and completely unsatisfying, because it hands the problem straight back to you. And there was a second axis nobody was testing: does the answer change between quantizations of the same model? K_M and K_XL are the same weights with different bit allocations, about a gigabyte apart on disk. On a card where a gigabyte is 4% of the total budget, that is not obviously a rounding error. So: two open questions, no answers, and a 4090 doing nothing at night. 2. How many values? Yes I could not sleep with this open. If I could not sleep, my computer wasn’t going to either. I built both quants at the same context size, wrote a harness that walks draft_num_predict from 0 to 15, three runs at each value, same prompt set every time, and left it running. Sixteen depths × two quants × three runs = 96 runs. Sixteen is more than anybody recommends testing. That is the point. Every guide says sweep 1 through 6; but if the useful range really ends around 6, I wanted to see what the other side of the wall looks like , because “don’t go past 6” and “past 6 your machine turns into a potato” are very different warnings, and only one of them makes you double-check your Modelfile before you walk away for the night. 3. The setup 3.1. The machine Intel Core i7–14700KF with 128 GB RAM and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 (24 GB VRAM) running on Ubuntu 24.04 with Ollama. Flash attention on, q8_0 KV cache, OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=1. That is the whole daemon-level story. Everything else that could move a number lives in the Modelfile below. 3.2. The sixteen builds In Ollama the MTP head is a DRAFT instruction in the Modelfile, not a second FROM. One line, pointing at the Q4_0 module you downloaded alongside the weights: FROM ./Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf DRAFT ./mtp-Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_0.gguf PARAMETER num_ctx 98304 PARAMETER num_batch 512 PARAMETER temperature 1.0 PARAMETER top_p 0.95 PARAMETER top_k 20 PARAMETER min_p 0.0 PARAMETER presence_penalty 0.0 PARAMETER repeat_penalty 1.0 PARAMETER draft_num_predict 5 Sixteen depths meant sixteen builds: same two .gguf files, one PARAMETER draft_num_predict apart, each tagged with its own depth so the harness could walk them by name. Thirty-two builds for the MTP benchmark (By Author) Thirty-two builds, actually (sixteen depths per quant). And there is the gigabyte the rest of this article turns on, sitting in the SIZE column: 17 GB against 18 GB. 3.3. What I held constant Sampling. Exactly as Qwen recommends for this family: the values in the Modelfile above, identical across all sixteen builds. 96K of context. Just because I can load either quant, with the MTP module resident, and stay fully on the GPU. MTP eats VRAM like everything else. In my experience, the moment any part of this model spills to CPU the measurement stops being about MTP and starts being about round-trip latency, and a benchmark that silently changes what it is measuring halfway through a sweep is worse than no benchmark. No vision projector. I left the mmproj out to keep this to one variable. 3.4. The benchmark All sixteen model configurations received the same instruction: You are a technical writing benchmark generator. Write a long, continuous, detailed explanation of how transformer-based LLMs decode text, including attention, KV cache, sampling, batching, and token prediction. Do not use markdown. Do not stop early. Continue with as much concrete detail as possible. Prose, not code, and markdown explicitly disabled (one text distribution across the whole sweep), so nothing downstream is a formatting artifact. The measurement. Completion tokens divided by the streaming window, where the window starts at the first token , not at the request. Prefill and model load are excluded by construction, so what you are looking at is decode throughput and nothing else. Time to first token is recorded separately, from request start to first streamed character. Four details that make the numbers worth arguing about: A 16-token warmup runs before every measured call and is thrown away. No cold-load contamination anywhere in the sweep. Model order is shuffled every epoch. If the room warms up, or the card throttles, or something drifts over eight hours of running, it does not land systematically on whichever model happened to be last in the list. Stopping is adaptive, not fixed. The harness keeps running epochs until every model has the same number of successful runs, there are no errors, and the cumulative generated volume across models agrees within 5% of the median (tolerating at most one outlier beyond 2σ). Minimum three epochs, maximum ten. It converged at three, which is why every point here is n=3. Failures abort, they do not get papered over. Two retries per call; if a model still fails, the run stops rather than write a partial epoch and quietly break the equal-run-count invariant. Every configuration in this article has three successes and zero errors. 3.5. What the numbers are not Three limits worth stating up front: Not long-context measurements. Time to first token sits around 316 ms across the sweep, which tells you the prompt is short relative to the window. The models are configured for 96K; the prompt did not fill it. Everything here is decode-bound behavior. Not your numbers. Absolute throughput on your machine will differ with card, driver, thermals and whatever else you have open. The community sweep linked above says it better than I can: the deltas are the durable part, not the absolutes. Not instrumented for VRAM. I confirmed the GPU/CPU split was 100% GPU for every configuration before each run, but I did not record it per configuration alongside the throughput numbers. Nothing here spilled to CPU; I just can’t hand you the table. The harness is standard library only (no dependencies, no framework), one file. If you want to reproduce this on your own card, here you are . 4. The whole curve Decode Throughput as a Function of Speculative Draft Depth for Two 4-Bit Quantizations (By Author) Both quants climb hard, peak around N=5, and then fall off a cliff into a region where enabling MTP is worse than never having touched it. Not slightly worse. At N=15 the K_XL build runs at 8.7 t/s against a 46.3 t/s baseline (a 5.3× slowdown ), with the model 100% resident on the GPU throughout (verified, not assumed). This is not spilling. It is the drafting itself. The good half first: Peak Throughput and Speedup at N=5, Both Quants (By Author) Roughly double, on both quants. That sits squarely inside the range Unsloth publishes for MTP on this family, so no surprise there. The surprise is everything to the right of the peak. 5. Where MTP stops paying Speedup Relative to Disabled Speculation Across Draft Depths (By Author) Here is the answer to the question I actually started with, and it is not a single number. K_XL goes underwater at N=8. K_M holds out until N=11. Same model. Same machine. Same prompt. Same night. The only difference is about a gigabyte of weights, and it is worth three steps of draft_num_predict . That is the part I had not seen written down anywhere, and it changes how you should read every recommendation in that table. “Use a low value” is not a property of the model. It is a property of the model and the quantization and the card and how much room is left after your context. A depth that is comfortable on K_M can already be past break-even on K_XL, on the identical machine, on the same afternoon. If you take one thing from this article: the safe depth is not a constant you can copy from a docs page. It moves with your build. 6. What the measurements actually say Forget the fit for a moment. Here is every candidate depth, as speedup over MTP off, on both builds (plus the average of the two) and, more usefully, the worse of the two, because on an unknown machine the floor matters more than the ceiling. Speedup at Every Candidate Depth, With Mean and Worst Case Across Builds (By Author) N=5 wins outright, four times over. Best on K_M. Best on K_XL. Best average. Best worst case. There is no criterion in this dataset under which something else is preferable. The two curves do not agree equally well, and that is worth being precise about. K_XL rises monotonically (1.43, 1.59, 1.65, 1.74, 1.82) and tops out cleanly at 5. K_M is jagged: it swings 0.3× or more between adjacent depths across the whole healthy band, which is more movement than the 5% separating its own peak from N=2. So the clean read on N=5 comes from K_XL, and K_M agrees with it without being able to resolve it on its own. Two builds landing in the same place is worth something. items.summary_html:
I Benchmarked Every MTP Depth on Qwen3.8–27B-UD-Q4_K_M/XL. Here You Are.Normal decoding is one forward pass per-token. That is the entire bottleneck of local inference.TL;DR

MTP on Qwen3.8–27B-UD-Q4 gives a genuine ~2× on a 4090: 48.5 → 96.2 t/s on K_M, 46.3 → 84.2 t/s on K_XL. The useful band for draft_num_predict is 2 to 5, and 5 is the pick: best on K_M, best on K_XL, best average, best worst case.

Above 5 both builds lose ground. Drafting more tokens does not raise how many get accepted per verification pass, so the extra drafts are pure cost.

Above 8 on K_XL, or 11 on K_M, you are actively destroying performance (up to 5.3× slower than not using MTP at all). Those two numbers are three apart, on the same model and the same card, and that is the whole reason “use a low value” was never a sufficient answer. The heavier quant breaks earlier. Your card will break somewhere else.

Seventeen Gigabytes of Weights Moved to Produce a Single Token (By Author, Powered by Gemini)

At 27B parameters and 4-bit weights on my RTX 4090, one decode step costs roughly 20.6 ms and produces exactly one token. That is where my ~48 tokens/s comes from, and no amount of clever prompting changes it.

The trick behind speculative decoding is that the forward pass is bound by memory bandwidth, not by compute. You are dragging seventeen gigabytes of weights across the memory bus to produce a single token. If you happened to have several candidate tokens sitting there, you could verify all of them in that same pass for nearly no extra cost, because the weights are already in flight.

Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) is where those candidates come from. unsloth/Qwen3.8–27B-GGUF ships with a small head trained to guess the next few tokens. The head drafts, the full model verifies. Every draft that matches what the model would have produced anyway is a free token. Every draft that doesn’t is thrown away, and you fall back to the one token you were going to get regardless.

Two things follow, and both matter for the rest of this article.

First, MTP is not a quality tradeoff. The verification step is what makes it safe: a drafted token only survives if the main model agrees with it. NVIDIA’s primer on the technique puts it plainly: when the draft is wrong, the target model just decodes normally, so the output is not degraded. This is not quantization. You are not trading precision for speed. You are trading VRAM for speed.

Second, it is not free. The draft head has to live in memory, the drafted tokens have to be generated, and the verification pass has to chew through all of them whether they are accepted or not. On the Unsloth model card, the MTP module for Qwen3.8–27B ships as a single Q4_0 file of about 1.37 GB (no separate MTP build per quantization). You download the same module whether you run UD-Q4_K_M, UD-Q4_K_XL or anything else, and it costs the same gigabyte and change either way.

On a 24 GB card, 1.37 GB is not pocket money. That is the whole tension.

1. The problem: everybody says “low,” nobody says how low

draft_num_predict N is the knob. It tells the runtime how many tokens to draft per verification pass. N=0 turns MTP off.

When I went looking for a starting value, every source agreed on the shape of the advice (keep it small, more is not better) and disagreed on the number.

Recommended Draft Depth by Source, and the Range They Span (By Author)

One, two, three, five, six. All of them are “low.” All of them come from people who know exactly what they are doing. The spread between smallest and largest is a factor of six, and every one of those pages tells you, correctly, that the right answer depends on your hardware.

Unsloth is the most explicit: try 1 through 6, keep whichever is fastest, and do not assume their starting number is optimal because performance is hardware-dependent.

Honest advice, and completely unsatisfying, because it hands the problem straight back to you. And there was a second axis nobody was testing: does the answer change between quantizations of the same model? K_M and K_XL are the same weights with different bit allocations, about a gigabyte apart on disk. On a card where a gigabyte is 4% of the total budget, that is not obviously a rounding error.

So: two open questions, no answers, and a 4090 doing nothing at night.

2. How many values? Yes

I could not sleep with this open. If I could not sleep, my computer wasn’t going to either.

I built both quants at the same context size, wrote a harness that walks draft_num_predict from 0 to 15, three runs at each value, same prompt set every time, and left it running. Sixteen depths × two quants × three runs = 96 runs.

Sixteen is more than anybody recommends testing. That is the point. Every guide says sweep 1 through 6; but if the useful range really ends around 6, I wanted to see what the other side of the wall looks like, because “don’t go past 6” and “past 6 your machine turns into a potato” are very different warnings, and only one of them makes you double-check your Modelfile before you walk away for the night.

3. The setup3.1. The machine

Intel Core i7–14700KF with 128 GB RAM and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 (24 GB VRAM) running on Ubuntu 24.04 with Ollama. Flash attention on, q8_0 KV cache, OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=1. That is the whole daemon-level story. Everything else that could move a number lives in the Modelfile below.

3.2. The sixteen builds

In Ollama the MTP head is a DRAFT instruction in the Modelfile, not a second FROM. One line, pointing at the Q4_0 module you downloaded alongside the weights:

FROM ./Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf
DRAFT ./mtp-Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_0.gguf
PARAMETER num_ctx 98304
PARAMETER num_batch 512
PARAMETER temperature 1.0
PARAMETER top_p 0.95
PARAMETER top_k 20
PARAMETER min_p 0.0
PARAMETER presence_penalty 0.0
PARAMETER repeat_penalty 1.0
PARAMETER draft_num_predict 5

Sixteen depths meant sixteen builds: same two .gguf files, one PARAMETER draft_num_predict apart, each tagged with its own depth so the harness could walk them by name.

Thirty-two builds for the MTP benchmark (By Author)

Thirty-two builds, actually (sixteen depths per quant). And there is the gigabyte the rest of this article turns on, sitting in the SIZE column: 17 GB against 18 GB.

3.3. What I held constant

Sampling. Exactly as Qwen recommends for this family: the values in the Modelfile above, identical across all sixteen builds.

96K of context. Just because I can load either quant, with the MTP module resident, and stay fully on the GPU. MTP eats VRAM like everything else. In my experience, the moment any part of this model spills to CPU the measurement stops being about MTP and starts being about round-trip latency, and a benchmark that silently changes what it is measuring halfway through a sweep is worse than no benchmark.

No vision projector. I left the mmproj out to keep this to one variable.

3.4. The benchmark

All sixteen model configurations received the same instruction:

You are a technical writing benchmark generator. Write a long, continuous,
detailed explanation of how transformer-based LLMs decode text, including
attention, KV cache, sampling, batching, and token prediction. Do not use
markdown. Do not stop early. Continue with as much concrete detail as possible.

Prose, not code, and markdown explicitly disabled (one text distribution across the whole sweep), so nothing downstream is a formatting artifact.

The measurement. Completion tokens divided by the streaming window, where the window starts at the first token, not at the request. Prefill and model load are excluded by construction, so what you are looking at is decode throughput and nothing else. Time to first token is recorded separately, from request start to first streamed character.

Four details that make the numbers worth arguing about:

  • A 16-token warmup runs before every measured call and is thrown away. No cold-load contamination anywhere in the sweep.
  • Model order is shuffled every epoch. If the room warms up, or the card throttles, or something drifts over eight hours of running, it does not land systematically on whichever model happened to be last in the list.
  • Stopping is adaptive, not fixed. The harness keeps running epochs until every model has the same number of successful runs, there are no errors, and the cumulative generated volume across models agrees within 5% of the median (tolerating at most one outlier beyond 2σ). Minimum three epochs, maximum ten. It converged at three, which is why every point here is n=3.
  • Failures abort, they do not get papered over. Two retries per call; if a model still fails, the run stops rather than write a partial epoch and quietly break the equal-run-count invariant. Every configuration in this article has three successes and zero errors.
3.5. What the numbers are not

Three limits worth stating up front:

  • Not long-context measurements. Time to first token sits around 316 ms across the sweep, which tells you the prompt is short relative to the window. The models are configured for 96K; the prompt did not fill it. Everything here is decode-bound behavior.
  • Not your numbers. Absolute throughput on your machine will differ with card, driver, thermals and whatever else you have open. The community sweep linked above says it better than I can: the deltas are the durable part, not the absolutes.
  • Not instrumented for VRAM. I confirmed the GPU/CPU split was 100% GPU for every configuration before each run, but I did not record it per configuration alongside the throughput numbers. Nothing here spilled to CPU; I just can’t hand you the table.

The harness is standard library only (no dependencies, no framework), one file. If you want to reproduce this on your own card, here you are.

4. The whole curveDecode Throughput as a Function of Speculative Draft Depth for Two 4-Bit Quantizations (By Author)

Both quants climb hard, peak around N=5, and then fall off a cliff into a region where enabling MTP is worse than never having touched it. Not slightly worse. At N=15 the K_XL build runs at 8.7 t/s against a 46.3 t/s baseline (a 5.3× slowdown), with the model 100% resident on the GPU throughout (verified, not assumed). This is not spilling. It is the drafting itself.

The good half first:

Peak Throughput and Speedup at N=5, Both Quants (By Author)

Roughly double, on both quants. That sits squarely inside the range Unsloth publishes for MTP on this family, so no surprise there. The surprise is everything to the right of the peak.

5. Where MTP stops payingSpeedup Relative to Disabled Speculation Across Draft Depths (By Author)

Here is the answer to the question I actually started with, and it is not a single number.

K_XL goes underwater at N=8. K_M holds out until N=11.

Same model. Same machine. Same prompt. Same night. The only difference is about a gigabyte of weights, and it is worth three steps of draft_num_predict.

That is the part I had not seen written down anywhere, and it changes how you should read every recommendation in that table. “Use a low value” is not a property of the model. It is a property of the model and the quantization and the card and how much room is left after your context. A depth that is comfortable on K_M can already be past break-even on K_XL, on the identical machine, on the same afternoon.

If you take one thing from this article: the safe depth is not a constant you can copy from a docs page. It moves with your build.

6. What the measurements actually say

Forget the fit for a moment. Here is every candidate depth, as speedup over MTP off, on both builds (plus the average of the two) and, more usefully, the worse of the two, because on an unknown machine the floor matters more than the ceiling.

Speedup at Every Candidate Depth, With Mean and Worst Case Across Builds (By Author)

N=5 wins outright, four times over. Best on K_M. Best on K_XL. Best average. Best worst case. There is no criterion in this dataset under which something else is preferable.

The two curves do not agree equally well, and that is worth being precise about. K_XL rises monotonically (1.43, 1.59, 1.65, 1.74, 1.82) and tops out cleanly at 5. K_M is jagged: it swings 0.3× or more between adjacent depths across the whole healthy band, which is more movement than the 5% separating its own peak from N=2. So the clean read on N=5 comes from K_XL, and K_M agrees with it without being able to resolve it on its own. Two builds landing in the same place is worth something. It is not two independent measurements.

One caveat on reading the ordering too closely: K_M dips to 1.50× at N=4, but K_XL’s N=4 is 1.74×, its second-best value in the sweep. The builds disagree there, which is the signature of run-to-run noise rather than a property of the depth. Anywhere from 2 to 5 is a defensible setting. Below 2 you are leaving speed on the table; above 5 you are paying for drafts nobody accepts.

So: the useful band is 2 to 5, the pick is 5.

7. The bill you pay on first-token latencyTime to First Token as a Function of Speculative Draft Depth (By Author)

Time to first token is flat at around 316 ms from N=0 through N=7 on both builds. In the healthy region, drafting costs you nothing on latency. You get the throughput and pay no entry fee.

Then it climbs: 526 ms on K_M at N=15 (+66%), 624 ms on K_XL (+97%). And look at where it starts climbing: K_XL departs at N=8, K_M at N=11. The same two numbers as the throughput cliff. Two independent metrics pointing at the same boundary is the closest thing to corroboration this dataset has.

The practical use: first-token latency is a free early-warning signal. If it starts rising as you raise N, you have already gone too far. You do not need to wait for a throughput measurement to tell you.

8. When to use MTP at all

This is the part the throughput numbers cannot answer, because on a 24 GB card MTP and context length draw from the same account. The draft module and its buffers are gigabytes you are not spending on KV cache. So “should I enable MTP” is really “what am I selling to pay for it,” and the answer depends on how you work.

I split my own AI-assisted development into two modes, and they want opposite things.

8.1. Unattended: the agent is working, I am notUnattended: the agent is working, I am not (By Author, Powered by Gemini)

I hand over a plan, a checklist, a set of specs, and I go do something else. The agent decomposes the work, spawns subagents, moves through tasks, updates state, and I read the result later.

Here the scarce resource is context, not speed. The agent needs room for the plan, the checklist, its own reasoning, the files it is touching, and the output it is about to write on top of all that. When it runs out it compacts, and if the window is too small it compacts so often that it never gets a clear run at the actual feature: you end up in a loop where nothing finishes. Meanwhile nobody is watching the tokens stream. The difference between 48 t/s and 96 t/s costs me nothing, because I am not in the room. Trading a gigabyte and a half of context for speed I will never observe is a bad deal.

Unattended work: keep the context. Skip MTP.

8.2. Attended: I am in the loop, and I am the one waitingAttended: I am in the loop, and I am the one waiting (By Author, Powered by ChatGPT)

This is babysitting mode. I am prompting in Claude Code or OpenCode, referencing the specific files that matter, defining the boundaries of the task myself: clearly and comprehensively, because in this mode that is my job.

Here the context requirement is genuinely smaller, and not as a compromise. When I review code I would rather read ten to twenty files properly than have something skim two hundred and hand me a summary. Or worse: watch a test suite I did not write go green over coverage I never checked, and push to main with a sense of safety I have not earned. Ten files I actually understand beats two hundred I have merely been near.

So the window is small on purpose, and the bottleneck moves somewhere completely different: to me, watching tokens appear. Every second of decode is a second of my attention burning. Doubling throughput here does not save the machine any work, it saves mine, and it is the difference between a tight iteration loop and one where I alt-tab away and lose the thread entirely.

Attended work: take the speed. Enable MTP.

The general principle, if you want one: MTP converts VRAM into decode speed. That is a good trade exactly when a human is waiting on the tokens, and a bad one when a machine is.

items.title: What’s left to engineer when the model is good?
items.summary: Our second book, AI Engineering for Production, launches October 20 When we published Building LLMs for Production in 2024, we thought we had written a book we could keep updating as the field evolved. We were wrong. Not about where the field was going, but about how much the engineering itself would change. In 2024, much of the work was still about getting more out of the LLM. Two years later, the model is only one component of the system. The field is more mature now, and so is the problem we wanted the book to solve. Rather than anchor another book too closely to today’s stack, we wanted to focus on the engineering problems that better models alone will not solve. So what began as an update became book number two: AI Engineering for Production, launching October 20. The question behind it is simple: once the model is already good, what actually gets a system the rest of the way to production? We also want to finish this book a little differently. Rather than show up on October 20 with a finished book, over the next few weeks, we will share our progress as we make the final passes, and we would genuinely like your help making it better. If there is a problem you think we have missed, something you want us to go deeper on, or a question you would want the book to answer, reply to any of those updates. We will be reading them as we fine-tune the final version and, wherever it makes the book stronger, working your feedback in. Then, on launch day, we are bringing everyone together. We will open up the book, show you the AI engineering stack we actually use today and the decisions behind it, and spend a big part of the session answering your technical questions live. Follow the book + join us on October 20 What’s left to engineer when the model is good? was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Our second book, AI Engineering for Production, launches October 20

When we published Building LLMs for Production in 2024, we thought we had written a book we could keep updating as the field evolved.

We were wrong.

Not about where the field was going, but about how much the engineering itself would change. In 2024, much of the work was still about getting more out of the LLM.

Two years later, the model is only one component of the system.

The field is more mature now, and so is the problem we wanted the book to solve. Rather than anchor another book too closely to today’s stack, we wanted to focus on the engineering problems that better models alone will not solve.

So what began as an update became book number two:

AI Engineering for Production, launching October 20.

The question behind it is simple: once the model is already good, what actually gets a system the rest of the way to production?

We also want to finish this book a little differently. Rather than show up on October 20 with a finished book, over the next few weeks, we will share our progress as we make the final passes, and we would genuinely like your help making it better.

If there is a problem you think we have missed, something you want us to go deeper on, or a question you would want the book to answer, reply to any of those updates. We will be reading them as we fine-tune the final version and, wherever it makes the book stronger, working your feedback in.

Then, on launch day, we are bringing everyone together. We will open up the book, show you the AI engineering stack we actually use today and the decisions behind it, and spend a big part of the session answering your technical questions live.

items.title: People ask how I manage 6 kids and caring for 3 relatives. I work a second job and barely get time to myself.
items.summary: Kaitlin Manns with her grandmother (second left), mom, and stepdad. She works as a health aide to all three. Courtesy of Kaitlin Manns Kaitlin Manns is a home health aide for three older family members. She works 38 hours a week at $18.50 an hour, taking care of them in turns. The mom-of-six, who also cares for two siblings, is employed at a bar and grill on weekends, too. This story is based on an interview with Kaitlin Manns, 33, a home health aide and server from Granite City, Illinois. It has been edited for length and clarity. My grandpa employed a carer before he died at 76. And my grandma, 76, mom, and stepdad, both 56 — all of whom have chronic medical conditions — had them, too. They were wonderful, but they ended up leaving for better-paid jobs. I didn't blame them, but it left our family struggling to find cover. So I decided to step in and do the job myself. It made sense because I've got a nurturing personality , and it felt like the right thing to do. What is your situation regarding long-term care for yourself or your loved ones? To share your story with a Business Insider reporter, please fill out this quick form . I work 2 jobs I qualified as a home health aide , a role that still requires monthly virtual training, and combined it with working as a server at a restaurant on weekends. Kaitlin Manns with her husband, Justice, and some young family members. Courtesy of Kaitlin Manns My days are pretty hectic, particularly because I have six kids aged between 2 and 13. Two of my siblings — both 9 — also live in my five-bedroom house, along with Mom and my stepdad. Grandma lives in her own home, about a 15-minute drive away. Thankfully, my husband, Justice, 28, is wonderful and really helps out. Still, he works mornings at a furniture rental company, so he's busy, too. Our schedule begins with him walking the oldest child two blocks to the school bus around 6:45 a.m. The others leave for their school, and I drop off Justice at his job. The state pays my salary Then I drive to the toddlers' day care before starting my caregiving around 9:30 a.m. I look after the three adults at separate times, helping them with things like showering, laundry, and doctors' appointments. On Mondays, I'll take care of Grandma and my stepdad. Tuesdays, it's my mom and stepdad. Wednesday is only my stepdad, Thursday is my grandma again, and I work for Mom on Friday morning. I usually put in 38 hours a week, earning $18.50 an hour, which is paid for by the state. Manns dressing up for her server job during the holidays. Courtesy of Kaitlin Manns On weekends, I work at least 23 hours as a server at a bar and grill, earning $7.50 an hour. But my pay is mostly tips. I can earn as much as $300 per shift. I love the job because it's a Mom-and-Pop business, and everybody knows each other. It's like being with friends. People often ask me how I manage to do it all. It's challenging at times, particularly because my grandma and stepdad have mobility and memory issues. I have little time to myself There's a lot of paperwork, too, such as getting Grandma approved for a scooter and a ramp. It takes a mixture of patience and organizational skills. It's very rewarding because I get to be with my loved ones all day. My job as a carer, big sister, and mom, plus the server work, leaves me little time for myself. However, I enjoy movies and reading on my Kindle before bed. I rest easy knowing I'm doing my very best for everyone. I'm paying my folks back for raising me while giving my kids a similar, loving childhood. Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
Kaitlin Manns with her grandmother (second left), mom, and stepdad. She works as a health aide to all three.

Courtesy of Kaitlin Manns

  • Kaitlin Manns is a home health aide for three older family members.
  • She works 38 hours a week at $18.50 an hour, taking care of them in turns.
  • The mom-of-six, who also cares for two siblings, is employed at a bar and grill on weekends, too.

This story is based on an interview with Kaitlin Manns, 33, a home health aide and server from Granite City, Illinois. It has been edited for length and clarity.

My grandpa employed a carer before he died at 76. And my grandma, 76, mom, and stepdad, both 56 — all of whom have chronic medical conditions — had them, too.

They were wonderful, but they ended up leaving for better-paid jobs. I didn't blame them, but it left our family struggling to find cover.

So I decided to step in and do the job myself. It made sense because I've got a nurturing personality, and it felt like the right thing to do.

What is your situation regarding long-term care for yourself or your loved ones? To share your story with a Business Insider reporter, please fill out this quick form.

I work 2 jobs

I qualified as a home health aide, a role that still requires monthly virtual training, and combined it with working as a server at a restaurant on weekends.

Kaitlin Manns with her husband, Justice, and some young family members.

Courtesy of Kaitlin Manns

My days are pretty hectic, particularly because I have six kids aged between 2 and 13. Two of my siblings — both 9 — also live in my five-bedroom house, along with Mom and my stepdad.

Grandma lives in her own home, about a 15-minute drive away.

Thankfully, my husband, Justice, 28, is wonderful and really helps out. Still, he works mornings at a furniture rental company, so he's busy, too.

Our schedule begins with him walking the oldest child two blocks to the school bus around 6:45 a.m. The others leave for their school, and I drop off Justice at his job.

The state pays my salary

Then I drive to the toddlers' day care before starting my caregiving around 9:30 a.m. I look after the three adults at separate times, helping them with things like showering, laundry, and doctors' appointments.

On Mondays, I'll take care of Grandma and my stepdad. Tuesdays, it's my mom and stepdad. Wednesday is only my stepdad, Thursday is my grandma again, and I work for Mom on Friday morning.

I usually put in 38 hours a week, earning $18.50 an hour, which is paid for by the state.

Manns dressing up for her server job during the holidays.

Courtesy of Kaitlin Manns

On weekends, I work at least 23 hours as a server at a bar and grill, earning $7.50 an hour. But my pay is mostly tips. I can earn as much as $300 per shift.

I love the job because it's a Mom-and-Pop business, and everybody knows each other. It's like being with friends.

People often ask me how I manage to do it all. It's challenging at times, particularly because my grandma and stepdad have mobility and memory issues.

I have little time to myself

There's a lot of paperwork, too, such as getting Grandma approved for a scooter and a ramp.

It takes a mixture of patience and organizational skills. It's very rewarding because I get to be with my loved ones all day.

My job as a carer, big sister, and mom, plus the server work, leaves me little time for myself. However, I enjoy movies and reading on my Kindle before bed.

I rest easy knowing I'm doing my very best for everyone. I'm paying my folks back for raising me while giving my kids a similar, loving childhood.

items.title: I booked a 5-week trip to visit my long-distance boyfriend. We broke up a month before, but I went anyway.
items.summary: I was hesitant to turn what was meant to be a visit with a long-distance partner into a solo trip, but I'm glad I did it. Jodie Hughes My long-distance partner and I broke up shortly before we were due to travel around the US together. I went on the trip alone. Family, friends, and kind strangers made it a lovely, cathartic adventure. The trip was an emotional roller coaster, culminating in a last meal with my ex to give me closure. Back in 2022, I got into a very long-distance relationship between Paris (the French one) and Boston (the American one). For about 18 months, we staggered along despite the thousands of miles between us. From the start, he seemed convinced that I needed to move to America if I wanted us to have a future. Despite my doubts, I began to consider relocating. I'd fallen for Boston, I live for adventure, and if I hated it, I could just… leave? By this point, the cracks were seriously showing, but we agreed I'd come to America for the summer, as a sort of trial run. We never got that far. Although we'd both questioned the future of our relationship, I was still stunned when he broke up with me a month before I was due to fly to the US. The flights were nonrefundable, and I love a solo trip , but I couldn't decide whether going it alone this time would be cathartic or catastrophic. I have family and friends in the US, though, and my flight was to San Diego, where one of my best friends lives, so I decided to go for it. Deep down, I hoped that maybe this experience would be more empowering than sad. Admittedly, the post-breakup trip had highs and lows My plans changed a lot by the time I left. Jodie Hughes I went from San Diego to San Francisco to Portland, enjoying several weeks with some of my favorite people, and it was the best tonic I could have hoped for. I was probably boring company at times; I spent many hours going over the countless reasons the relationship was never meant to last. But my nearest and dearest listened to me, and laughed with me, and took me on all kinds of adventures to the most gorgeous corners of California and Oregon. It's pretty hard to be sad when you're having that much fun with people you love. Seeing a lot of natural beauty with people I love helped heal me. Jodie Hughes The trickier part of the trip came toward the end, when I'd planned to spend a week in Boston . My first challenge was logistical: I now had nowhere to stay in one of America's most expensive cities, and, as usual, my travel budget was basically nonexistent. So I put out a candid appeal on a Facebook group for female travelers , sharing about my breakup and offering to later host someone in Paris in return for them hosting me in Boston. I got several incredibly kind responses and eventually connected with a single mom who generously let me stay with me for several nights. In the end, I'd been able to make the best of a strange situation I was able to make changes to my trip to make it work for me, thanks to family, friends, and a kind stranger from Facebook. Jodie Hughes Accommodation crisis averted, I set about exploring every nook and cranny of Boston. I hung out with lovely people, saw a lot of beautiful sights, and ate incredible food — including a Boston-cream doughnut I still think about. However, I wasn't prepared for how strange it would feel to spend day after day traipsing alone around the city I'd imagined building a life in. My trip wasn't always easy, but it was cathartic. Jodie Hughes I also made the mistake of going to see a ludicrously emotional Pixar movie and nearly had to walk out because I was sobbing so hard. I only wanted the popcorn, for crying out loud. (That liquid-y "butter" on tap might be America's greatest invention.) I'd like to say "Inside Out 2" was the peak of the emotional turbulence, but that came in the form of a dinner with my ex, right before my return to Paris. It was pretty nerve-racking, and I hardly touched my food, but it was exactly the closure I'd dubiously hoped for. I was still working through the blow to my ego, and the indignation of the way everything had unfolded, but sitting across the table from this man I'd shed all those tears over, it was glaringly, gloriously obvious to me that the breakup had been the best call for us both. Ultimately, when it comes to going solo on a trip you'd planned with an ex, I would advise approaching with caution. It wasn't always easy; emotions ran high. But it was, overall, an incredible experience — more deeply healing than I could have hoped. And yes … a pretty damn empowering one, too. Read the original article on Business Insider
