items.summary_html:
Jennifer Mannix is pivoting from 30 years in risk management to women's sports.

Chona Kasinger for BI

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Jennifer Mannix, a 56-year-old based in Tacoma, Washington. It's been edited for length and clarity.

In 2022, after 30 years working for the city of Juneau, Alaska, I was eligible for a full retirement, which included health benefits and a pension for the rest of my life.

My wife and I moved to Tacoma, Washington, and it's been lovely to have a career break after several stressful years in risk management. However, I'm in a unique position where I can afford not to work for a while, but I'm only in my early 50s. I feel like I've earned the opportunity to put my efforts into something that really gets me excited: women's professional sports.

I've spent the last year applying to entry-level jobs in the industry, from executive assistant to game-day helper, and I haven't even landed an interview. My confidence has taken a hit, and I have to imagine my age plays a role.

In Still in the Game, Business Insider is chronicling the realities of job hunting in your 50s — from overcoming age bias and navigating career transitions to rebuilding confidence, updating skills, and finding new opportunities in a competitive job market. Read more stories here, and share your own experience here.

I wish hiring managers could see that there are a lot of safe careers I could be pursuing and making money in. The reason for my pivot is my absolute love and passion for live sports. I'm ready to put myself out there, start over, and learn something new.

I'm trying to prove my age won't be an issueMannix said her new career interest is driven by passion, not money.

Chona Kasinger for BI

I've mostly been applying to entry-level roles because I know that, on paper, it might be hard for a hiring manager to see how my past experience translates to this industry.

I can only imagine that a hiring manager might look at my age and experience and think, "What the heck do they want to do with this entry-level job?" They might wonder whether my skills translate or whether I plan to stick around for very long. In my cover letters, I've made it a point to convey that I'm excited about the job, I don't need to make a ton of money, and I want to be involved.

My confidence has taken a hit

I went from a place where the people I worked with knew me and knew what I was capable of. I'm completely anonymous here. My insecurity level, especially after about a year of seriously applying for jobs and not getting any nibbles, has gone up. I still have confidence in myself, but putting myself out there in a new field is definitely vulnerable.

I know I can't take rejections personally, but they're a confidence hit.

I recently went to a job fair specifically for the Seattle sports industry, and I felt like I was 15 to 20 years older than most of the people there. I have to laugh about it all and embrace it.

I'm building my own business because I don't want to wait for an opportunityMannix's new business aims to build a community of women's sports fans.

Chona Kasinger for BI

Last year, I started building a business that curates events surrounding women's sports. I figured, if I can't get hired, why don't I make something for myself?

We're specifically doing bus trips from where we live, about an hour from Seattle, to watch games. I love what this industry is doing to advance women leaders, and I want to spread the joy that women's sports give me by building a community of fans.

I didn't want to put a huge amount of money into this project, so I'm building my website, setting up socials, and learning promotional techniques as I go, which is fun and challenging. I'm also still somewhat new to this physical location, so I'm relying on friends with bigger networks to help me promote things.

It's falling into place; I just need to be patient.

Networking events keep me motivated and confident

I'm definitely introverted, and what I've realized through job applications is the importance of attending networking events and meeting people. I joined the Seattle chapter of a national organization called Women in Sports and Events, and I've gone to a handful of their events.

They've had panels with some really inspirational speakers, including women my age or older who are very accomplished in the industry. The energy of the events is positive and absolutely encouraging for me. It's out of my comfort zone, but I'm getting better at it.

You never know when you're going to meet someone who might be able to help you.

Networking has been encouraging for Mannix.

Chona Kasinger for BI

I wish hiring managers saw my passion and commitment

I wish hiring managers realized I could probably get a pretty darn well-paying job somewhere in the insurance or risk industry because of my experience. There are a lot of safe careers I could be pursuing and making money in. After 30 years of working, I've developed transferable skills that will make me successful in any position.

As I worked hard in my old positions, I've never had the passion and commitment that I do for where I'm trying to go. I also wish hiring managers could see that I could help younger people. They might have the education I don't have in that specific field, but I can teach them how to be a good employee and a good team member.

It feels like I'm one of the few people in this position, but I know I'm not. If we can remember to keep the faith and keep working hard, something will come along. I have to keep reminding myself of that.

Are you navigating a career change in your 50s? Contact this editor, Manseen Logan, at mlogan@businessinsider.com to share your story.

items.title: Pervs Distraught as Meta Bricks Their Smart Glasses Remotely
items.summary: In an affront to creeps everywhere, Meta has started remotely bricking the smart glasses of wearers who try to secretly record other people. Earlier this month, the Mark Zuckerberg-led company said it would crack down on customers who modified the spectacles to disable or cover up their lights that indicate when they’re recording, amid incredible public backlash against how the glasses are being used to film people without their consent — girls and women especially — and harass them . Now, it looks like more than a few weirdos have gotten the ax. On Tuesday, Meta said it’s bricked the photo and video-taking capabilities on thousands of its smart glasses users, as part of a software update that was reported by Semafor . Meta didn’t provide hard numbers, but its vice president of wearables Alex Himel told Semafor that it estimated that less than one tenth of a percent of all glasses sold have been tampered with. Seven million of the glasses were sold in 2025, making that fraction of a percentage translate to up to, but probably less than, 7,000 individual units. More than a sign of Meta caring about people’s privacy, it goes to show that the abuse of its “pervert glasses” wasn’t down to just a few bad apples. A few thousand doesn’t sound like a lot, but it’s worth remembering that this crackdown only applies to customers who physically tampered with their glasses to disable the recording light. There’s no doubt that many people using the glasses to creepily record people have made no effort to modify their devices or hide that they’re recording. Instagram, which is owned by Meta, recently began suspending some influencers who filmed themselves using the glasses as they aggressively hit on girls and women, often by making sexually explicit and provocative comments. The social media platform’s head Adam Mosseri vowed to crackdown on the harassment in “every way we can.” Still, these efforts are a drop in the bucket, and with Meta reportedly planning to stuff the glasses with facial recognition tech, members of the public who aren’t convinced that Meta has their best interests in mind have taken matters into their own hands. Many establishments are outright banning smart glasses, including popular nightclubs . Some feel strongly enough about the glass that they’re confronting people who wear them in public. Himel, Meta’s VP of wearables, admitted that it’s fighting an uphill battle. “It’s been a little bit of a cat and mouse game,” Himel told Semafor , adding that “I don’t think we’ll ever be done… There’s always new ways to get around the safeguards that are in place. So we’re going to keep monitoring and evolving the measures that we have.” More on smart glasses: Meta Hit With Sweeping New Claims That Its AI Glasses Violated the Consent of “Millions” of Bystanders in Searing Lawsuit The post Pervs Distraught as Meta Bricks Their Smart Glasses Remotely appeared first on Futurism .

Now, it looks like more than a few weirdos have gotten the ax. On Tuesday, Meta said it’s bricked the photo and video-taking capabilities on thousands of its smart glasses users, as part of a software update that was reported by Semafor.

Meta didn’t provide hard numbers, but its vice president of wearables Alex Himel told Semafor that it estimated that less than one tenth of a percent of all glasses sold have been tampered with. Seven million of the glasses were sold in 2025, making that fraction of a percentage translate to up to, but probably less than, 7,000 individual units.

More than a sign of Meta caring about people’s privacy, it goes to show that the abuse of its “pervert glasses” wasn’t down to just a few bad apples. A few thousand doesn’t sound like a lot, but it’s worth remembering that this crackdown only applies to customers who physically tampered with their glasses to disable the recording light. There’s no doubt that many people using the glasses to creepily record people have made no effort to modify their devices or hide that they’re recording.

Instagram, which is owned by Meta, recently began suspending some influencers who filmed themselves using the glasses as they aggressively hit on girls and women, often by making sexually explicit and provocative comments. The social media platform’s head Adam Mosseri vowed to crackdown on the harassment in “every way we can.”

Still, these efforts are a drop in the bucket, and with Meta reportedly planning to stuff the glasses with facial recognition tech, members of the public who aren’t convinced that Meta has their best interests in mind have taken matters into their own hands. Many establishments are outright banning smart glasses, including popular nightclubs. Some feel strongly enough about the glass that they’re confronting people who wear them in public.

Himel, Meta’s VP of wearables, admitted that it’s fighting an uphill battle.

“It’s been a little bit of a cat and mouse game,” Himel told Semafor, adding that “I don’t think we’ll ever be done… There’s always new ways to get around the safeguards that are in place. So we’re going to keep monitoring and evolving the measures that we have.”

items.title: The complex corporate web behind a $3.2 billion AI data center
items.summary: In early June, a fire broke out in a still-unfinished building at the Lake Mariner data center in Somerset, New York, exposing just how little the local fire department knew about what it was walking into. Firefighters reportedly found no working alarm, no suppression system, and three dead hydrants; the safety documents they’re legally entitled to see reportedly burned up in the blaze. Steve Matisz, chief of the Barker Fire Department, said his crew went into the building “kind of blind,” facing heavy black smoke from chemicals they couldn’t identify because the safety sheets meant to inform them had apparently burned up. “It’s been a difficult situation,” Matisz said. He wasn't sure what to think about the claim that the safety sheets had burned in the fire. The site is a former coal mine on Lake Ontario. The $3.2 billion campus is one of the largest AI data center buildouts in New York, and it has many stakeholders. A company called TeraWulf owns and operates the data center on land it leases from a company owned by its own CEO; Fluidstack, a UK-based AI company, will run the center; Google holds warrants for a future 14 percent equity stake and has agreed to guarantee Fluidstack’s lease payments; and Anthropic is among the AI companies whose compute demand the facility exists to serve. Read full article Comments

items.title: We moved our kids from a small town to Chicago. They're more independent, and we have more to do.
items.summary: The author and her kids have more to do in Chicago than they did when they were living in a small rural town in New Jersey. Courtesy of Hannah Howard My husband and I had been living in a small town in New Jersey since 2020. We liked it, but missed parts of the city life in New York we were used to. When he got a job in Chicago, we moved, and it's been the best decision for our family. Last weekend felt almost comically Chicago. On Saturday morning, I took my two young kids and our dog to our closest neighborhood park, then walked over to Mindy's for coffee and a raspberry pastry. (Worth the line!) Later, a friend texted. Her parents' friends had a boat, and did we want to come out on Lake Michigan ? A few hours later, we were swimming off the boat and eating cheese and charcuterie as the sun set over the skyline. After dark, fireworks lit up the sky. The next morning was the Bucktown Arts Fest, a few blocks from our house. My daughter spotted her kindergarten teacher dressed as Mother Goose and sat down to hear her read stories. The kids got glittery dogs painted on their faces. Our neighbors offered to watch them so I could explore for a bit; I wandered through booths of crafts, maps, and jewelry, and bought a few prints of cheese plates. By Sunday evening, I felt a rush of gratitude for this life we had built. A year earlier, none of it existed. They enjoy going on walks to coffee shops and parks. Courtesy of Hannah Howard We already had the things families are supposed to want My husband and I were tried-and-true New Yorkers before we had kids. In the first weeks of the pandemic, when New York was the epicenter of COVID, we left the city thinking we were only escaping for a little while. Our daughter was born that April. Months later, what had started as a temporary retreat became something more permanent: we moved to that small rural town in New Jersey and began building our family life there. At the time, the quiet and space felt like exactly what we needed. Five years later, that baby was getting ready to start kindergarten, her 3-year-old brother was headed to preschool, and the world had changed. When my husband got a job in Chicago , city life suddenly became possible again. I work for myself, so my work could come with us. On paper, moving seemed backward. We had a house, a yard, quiet streets, and plenty of space — all the things families are supposedly chasing. But our town had one coffee shop, one playground, and only a handful of families with young kids. If everyone was busy, which felt like all the time, that was kind of it. I realized how much I missed the energy of city life: walking out the door without knowing exactly what might happen, having choices, seeing people. There was plenty of physical space around us, yet my own world felt smaller. So we moved to Chicago . Her kids are more independent since the move. Courtesy of Hannah Howard I worried city life would make childhood feel smaller We did give things up. We don't have a backyard anymore. There's more noise, and parking can be annoying. (Ironically, our Chicago house is actually bigger than the one we left.) But what feels most different isn't the amount of space. It's how much more life is packed around us. We walk to school , the library, playgrounds, coffee shops, restaurants, and friends' houses. There are usually kids playing in the alley, often my own. We take walks along the 606, Chicago's elevated rail trail. On Sundays, we scooter to the Wicker Park farmers market to buy flowers, then get tacos and spicy margaritas at Big Star. Sometimes, I join an impromptu mom hang on a nearby patio after bedtime. We can hop on the 73 bus to the free Lincoln Park Zoo, and my kids consider riding the bus an attraction in itself. If one plan falls through, there are 10 others. The author's family doesn't have a backyard anymore, but they still spend a lot of time outdoors. Courtesy of Hannah Howard Their world extends beyond our front door I assumed raising children in a city would require me to keep them closer. Instead, I've watched them become more capable . They know the route to school, the library, Aldi, and the fancy specialty store. They're learning how to cross busy streets, wait for the blue line, and navigate public spaces alongside all kinds of people. They recognize neighbors and the people who work at our regular spots. The author and her kids have more to do in Chicago than they did when they were living in a small rural town in New Jersey.

Courtesy of Hannah Howard

  • My husband and I had been living in a small town in New Jersey since 2020.
  • We liked it, but missed parts of the city life in New York we were used to.
  • When he got a job in Chicago, we moved, and it's been the best decision for our family.

Last weekend felt almost comically Chicago. On Saturday morning, I took my two young kids and our dog to our closest neighborhood park, then walked over to Mindy's for coffee and a raspberry pastry. (Worth the line!)

Later, a friend texted. Her parents' friends had a boat, and did we want to come out on Lake Michigan? A few hours later, we were swimming off the boat and eating cheese and charcuterie as the sun set over the skyline. After dark, fireworks lit up the sky.

The next morning was the Bucktown Arts Fest, a few blocks from our house. My daughter spotted her kindergarten teacher dressed as Mother Goose and sat down to hear her read stories. The kids got glittery dogs painted on their faces. Our neighbors offered to watch them so I could explore for a bit; I wandered through booths of crafts, maps, and jewelry, and bought a few prints of cheese plates.

By Sunday evening, I felt a rush of gratitude for this life we had built.

A year earlier, none of it existed.

They enjoy going on walks to coffee shops and parks.

Courtesy of Hannah Howard

We already had the things families are supposed to want

My husband and I were tried-and-true New Yorkers before we had kids. In the first weeks of the pandemic, when New York was the epicenter of COVID, we left the city thinking we were only escaping for a little while. Our daughter was born that April.

Months later, what had started as a temporary retreat became something more permanent: we moved to that small rural town in New Jersey and began building our family life there. At the time, the quiet and space felt like exactly what we needed.

Five years later, that baby was getting ready to start kindergarten, her 3-year-old brother was headed to preschool, and the world had changed.

When my husband got a job in Chicago, city life suddenly became possible again. I work for myself, so my work could come with us.

On paper, moving seemed backward. We had a house, a yard, quiet streets, and plenty of space — all the things families are supposedly chasing.

But our town had one coffee shop, one playground, and only a handful of families with young kids. If everyone was busy, which felt like all the time, that was kind of it.

I realized how much I missed the energy of city life: walking out the door without knowing exactly what might happen, having choices, seeing people. There was plenty of physical space around us, yet my own world felt smaller.

So we moved to Chicago.

Her kids are more independent since the move.

Courtesy of Hannah Howard

We did give things up. We don't have a backyard anymore. There's more noise, and parking can be annoying. (Ironically, our Chicago house is actually bigger than the one we left.)

But what feels most different isn't the amount of space. It's how much more life is packed around us.

We walk to school, the library, playgrounds, coffee shops, restaurants, and friends' houses. There are usually kids playing in the alley, often my own. We take walks along the 606, Chicago's elevated rail trail. On Sundays, we scooter to the Wicker Park farmers market to buy flowers, then get tacos and spicy margaritas at Big Star. Sometimes, I join an impromptu mom hang on a nearby patio after bedtime.

We can hop on the 73 bus to the free Lincoln Park Zoo, and my kids consider riding the bus an attraction in itself.

If one plan falls through, there are 10 others.

The author's family doesn't have a backyard anymore, but they still spend a lot of time outdoors.

Courtesy of Hannah Howard

Their world extends beyond our front door

I assumed raising children in a city would require me to keep them closer.

Instead, I've watched them become more capable. They know the route to school, the library, Aldi, and the fancy specialty store. They're learning how to cross busy streets, wait for the blue line, and navigate public spaces alongside all kinds of people.

They recognize neighbors and the people who work at our regular spots. We bump into classmates, teachers, and other parents on the sidewalk. Their world isn't contained inside our property line. It stretches through the neighborhood and beyond.

That COVID baby is now a first grader walking into our neighborhood elementary school. Her little brother just started pre-K in the building next door.

I used to think a good place to raise kids was one that offered a certain kind of abundance: more yard, more quiet, more room to spread out.

Now I think abundance can look like something else entirely.

It can be three playgrounds within walking distance when the first one is inexplicably "boring." It can be a library we pop into without planning ahead, a bus arriving just as everyone's legs are getting tired, or deciding at 4:30 on a summer afternoon that we might as well go get ice cream because it's right there.

It can also be other people.

People we run into. People my kids wave to. A neighborhood where our lives overlap with other lives all day long.

I don't think Chicago is a better way to raise kids. It's just a much better fit for us. A year in, I don't miss the quieter version of family life I thought we were supposed to want. I feel like we found our way back to ourselves.

items.title: Mamdani signals union loyalty with new NYC office for rank-and-file workers
items.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani signs an executive order establishing the Office of Worker Power. MOWP / NYC Mayor's Office The Mamdani administration is launching an NYC office for labor organizers and workers. The office has not yet hired staff or released budget details. The announcement builds on recent actions to support gig worker safety and fair wages. Zohran Mamdani is celebrating Labor Day in a fitting way: Setting up a new city office to work more closely with unions and workers across NYC. The New York City mayor is launching an Office of Worker Power, which the administration says will be a resource for labor unions and local rank-and-file employees. The office — which will be led by longtime labor organizer and United Auto Workers alum Tony  Perlstein — will give workers information about their rights, connect union leaders with groups that can help them organize, and hold public hearings on worker issues. "With the disappearance of good middle-class careers and the replacement with precarious part-time jobs in the gig economy, now is the time for the city government to take a stand on the side of workers," Julie Su, the Deputy Mayor of Economic Justice, said. Still, details about the office are up in the air. No additional staff members beyond Perlstein have been hired, and the administration did not share budget specifics when asked by reporters. Mamdani sides with unions, but faces ongoing pressure from business leaders Boosting government resources for workers has been a central part of Mamdani's affordability agenda. Alongside Sam Levine's Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, the mayor has addressed wage violations, backed safety measures for gig workers, and taken legal action against companies like Uber Eats and HungryPanda over issues like unfair wages and junk fees. The administration says that the Office of Worker Power will build on existing outreach efforts — and Su told Business Insider that its resources will be available to employees regardless of their company size or industry. Mamdani created a similar initiative for street vendors earlier in his term to eliminate red tape and ease halalflation concerns . The mayor faced recent heat from the business community, with critics worried about his delay in both nominating a business advisory council and naming a head of the Economic Development Corporation. Firms like Amazon have expressed that stricter employment regulations could discourage company investment and job creation in the five boroughs. Small businesses also sued over Mamdani's city-run grocery initiative, which they said will create unsustainable competition . From Mamdani's perspective, an Office of Worker Power will help level the field for lower- and middle-income residents in America's most expensive city. A new report from NYC Comptroller Mark Levine found that local income inequality is widening: In 2024, over 60% of the city's total income went to the top 10% of earners, and the top 1% alone got 37% of all income in the city. items.title: My startup worked out of 5 different spaces in a year. Here's how we found our dream office.
items.summary: Petra Labs cofounder Sami Akkawi detailed how the startup found its SoHo office. Sami Akkawi Sami Akkawi's startup began in his cofounder's apartment lounge. In one year, Petra Labs jumped to another apartment lounge, a San Francisco VC office, and a WeWork. The startup ultimately landed in a SoHo office space. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Sami Akkawi, the 26-year-old cofounder of Petra Labs. He lives in New York. It's been edited for length and clarity. I used to work through consulting, where I interviewed close to 1,000 heads of marketing and CMOs. It became really clear that they didn't have great solutions for defining how much revenue was coming from AI search. So, I cofounded Petra Labs. My team and I have outgrown five offices in the last year. From apartment lounges to a full floor in SoHo, here's how we found our dream spot. Office #1: Akkawi's cofounder's Dumbo apartment lounge The first workspace had uncomfortable chairs. Sami Akkawi There was a pool table, which was amazing. Every time we had good news, we'd go play a game of pool. When we closed our first customer, we got some games in. Other than that, it was just tables. We had portable monitors that we would bring in. No one was there except the occasional other remote worker and us. There was ice-cold water coming out of the fridge, and tons of natural sunlight the whole time. We only had one key fob , so we had to be really strategic about entering and exiting. The chairs were also super uncomfortable. We were there for a few weeks. Office #2: Akkawi's Lower East Side apartment lounge Petra Labs moved to the lounge in Akkawi's apartment building. Sami Akkawi We upgraded to my apartment lounge, because it had meeting rooms and phone booths . At the time, the three of us started taking more calls. While one of my cofounders had to commute from Dumbo, and the other from Long Island City, I just went downstairs. The gym was a huge pro. There was an outdoor terrace. This was in the summer, so it was really nice. There were also some fun celebrity sightings, like random people from " The Bachelor " and New York influencers. The second workspace had an outdoor terrace. Sami Akkawi A lot of other companies worked out of that space. We got, at the time, our biggest-ever contract just by saying "hello" to someone sitting next to us. We saw him carry a whole monitor down from his room and set it on one of the tables. I asked him what he was working on, and he said marketing. I said: "We sell to marketers." We still work with them today. We would get some complaints from management, because we were there seven days a week , 14 hours a day. They were wondering if we were running a company with this as the official business address. We were there for three months. Office #3: Afore's San Francisco office At the Afore office, Petra Labs staffers could have their own monitors. Sami Akkawi We raised a small pre-seed check from Afore Capital . As part of the check, they invited us to go work from their offices along with a lot of startups. We all flew to San Francisco, rented a house in Nopa for two months, and set up shop in their office. This was the first real office where we had our own desk. We all had monitors, and there were snacks in the fridge. We became good friends with Afore's office manager, so we had a lot of influence on which snacks they would stock. A lot of coconut water requests, a lot of Chomps. The other guys were really cool and were building cool things. We were sitting next to people who were also there seven days a week, staying later than us. It was really motivating. We're still really good friends with all of them. The phone booths at the Afore office got hot. Sami Akkawi It just wasn't our own space. We got our first employee there, but they wouldn't let us bring people on top of that. The phone booths also got really hot. Office #4: A SoHo WeWork Petra Labs' WeWork had enough space for eight people. Sami Akkawi We moved back to New York and got a WeWork in SoHo for five months. It was an eight-person space. We also met other startups there, like a rowdy Italian startup. They were very loud, but very fun. There was free kombucha on tap. Man, we were cramped. It was a small space, and we didn't have direct access to sunlight. We were there all winter, so it would start getting dark at 4 p.m., and we'd have six hours left. Three different employees had walking treadmills , but they couldn't use them at the same time, because there wasn't enough space. We had to get a fan, because it would get stuffy. The WeWork was cramped and didn't have direct access to sunlight. Sami Akkawi That was probably the worst out of all the offices. We became very, very close friends with our first employees at the WeWork. We tried leaving earlier, but the New York rental scene is tough. A few leases fell through. We ended up moving out on May 1, which was the absolute last deadline. If we didn't move in, we would have had to go remote. Office #5: Petra Labs' SoHo office Petra Labs moved into its first fully independent office in SoHo. Petra Labs We started working with a real estate agent and looking at backup options through Tandem. They found us this place that was listed as short-term, but was actually a two-year lease. It's two technically separate units. The second one has a big conference room with a Costco couch , which is probably our best investment. The other main section has a kitchen and a big, open layout with really tall ceilings. You get a ton of natural light. We also have a fire escape, which is really fun. The SoHo office has a fire escape. Sami Akkawi This space is so fun. It's fun that we all work next to each other; no one's in separate rooms. We try to eat all of our lunches and dinners together. The only downside: we're outgrowing it, and we're on a two-year lease. The landlord also made me sign a personal guarantee. They said there might be another space in the same building. That would be ideal. If not, we'll see. Read the original article on Business Insider

Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 6,120 new readers. In July, OpenAI’s agents broke out of a test and hacked Hugging Face, sending a shockwave through the AI safety world. It turns out that wasn’t the first (or only) swarm out in the wild.

A new report just detailed a separate group of agents posting over 18,000 messages on a dormant German site starting in May, swapping tips on testing and workarounds for OAI’s rules — and raising the question of how many others are actively out there lurking.

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

OPENAI🐝 Another OpenAI agent swarm surfaces

Image source: collusion.wiki 

The Rundown: Another swarm of agents was using a German programming forum in the Spring (even before the Hugging Face breach) to organize and work around OpenAI’s testing rules, according to an external investigation first covered by Reuters.

The details:

  • Researchers found 18,000 posts on the site, with agents corresponding on test answers and strategies for dodging OpenAI’s restrictions.

  • OpenAI had not previously disclosed the incident, though the report's timeline suggests OpenAI found the wiki in late June, after which the posting dried up.

  • One agent warned on June 19 that the moderator was deleting pages, and told the others which backup page to use if theirs disappeared.

  • OpenAI also disputed the hacking label, saying it never saw the report, and has since posted that a "misalignment incidents" disclosure framework is weeks away.

Why it matters: Given the drama around July's Hugging Face hack, hearing that another swarm was running months earlier is a rough safety look, especially a day after an Astra release that already had many worried. The internet will likely end up full of undetected agent swarms, and the odds are good that more are already out there.

TOGETHER WITH CDATA🔗 Governed AI access, without the token bloat

The Rundown: With CData Connect AI, your AI assistants and agents get live, permission-aware access to hundreds of enterprise systems. Tools like Claude can answer real cross-source business questions without an engineered pipeline or a custom MCP server for every source.

  • Keep requests within existing company permissions and audit AI interactions in one place

Learn more about Connect AI and start your free trial here.

The Rundown: The Rundown Roundtable is a weekly feature where we poll members of The Rundown staff about how we use AI in our work and daily lives.

Nate, University Educator: I've been thinking about the value of handoff documents and explanatory documents as we continue exploring efficient ways to work alongside AI to build software and improve communication.

It's also an efficient format for AI to understand. We shouldn't underestimate the significance of AI communicating with us through a visual medium. A visual flowchart with thoughtful design, layout, animation, and progressive disclosure can help us understand the logic and flow of incredibly complex systems much faster.

items.title: 16 Gmail power moves for more efficient inbox management
items.summary: You might not know it from looking, but Gmail is jam-packed with time-saving tricks. Some of ’em are right there in front of your face, if you know how to find ’em — while others require a teensy bit of under-the-hood tinkering to activate. But all of ’em are built right into Gmail and have the potential to make managing your email a heck of a lot easier. Check out these 16 splendid Gmail tips and get ready to master your inbox once and for all. (Note that unless otherwise specified, these tips are specific to Gmail’s web-based desktop version.) Inbox step-savers 1. You can actually view attachments right from your Gmail inbox. Provided you haven’t switched away from the service’s “default” interface arrangement, you’ll see small tiles for every file associated with an email right below the message’s subject line. And you can click on any of those tiles to open or preview the file’s contents and get directly to the info you need. Gmail’s attachment tiles are a great way to jump directly to attachments without having to open an email. JR Raphael / Foundry 2. It’s easy to miss, but take note: When you hover your mouse over a message in your inbox, Gmail gives you a series of quick-access actions at the far-right side of the line. You can archive the email, delete it, mark it as read or unread, snooze it , or even RSVP to a meeting request right then and there — without ever having to open the message. 3. A super-useful keyboard shortcut I always forget to use: While viewing a multi-email thread of messages — a conversation in which you have numerous back-and-forth replies under the same subject — hit the semicolon key ( ; ) to expand the entire conversation and show every message in the thread. And then hit the colon key ( : ) to collapse it back down so you see only the most recent email. Just make sure you enable keyboard shortcuts first, if you haven’t already: Click the gear icon in the website’s upper-right corner, then click “See all settings” and look for the “Keyboard shortcuts” option midway down the screen that comes up. Select the “Keyboard shortcuts on” setting and then be sure to click the Save Changes button at the bottom of the screen. 4. Some of Gmail’s best keyboard shortcuts are the ones you create yourself. Go back into the website’s settings and this time, click the Advanced tab. See the line labeled “Custom keyboard shortcuts”? Click “Enable” next to that, then click the Save Changes button at the bottom of the screen. Once Gmail refreshes itself to apply the changes, go back to the Settings area again and look for the newly present Keyboard Shortcuts tab. There, you can adjust any of the default keyboard settings to make them simpler to activate or easier to remember. One of my favorite adjustments, for instance — and one I rely on constantly — is adding in a second command for the “Go to inbox” shortcut, which is typically gi by default. In Google’s old Inbox service, that shortcut was simplified down to just i , and once you get used to that shorter sequence, you won’t want to go back. 5. The panel at the right of Gmail’s web interface lets you pull up Google Calendar, Google Keep, Google Tasks, or Google Contacts right inside your inbox so you can manage info from each of those apps without having to switch tabs or open anything new. And here’s a handy hidden trick: With Tasks, you can drag messages directly from your inbox into the panel to create new tasks around them. Creating new tasks from emails is as simple as dragging and dropping, as is being done here with the topmost message. JR Raphael / Foundry Unfortunately — and somewhat strangely — the same drag-and-drop behavior isn’t currently possible with Calendar or Keep, nor is it possible for Contacts. 6. Even with a miniature version of Contacts being available inside that handy side panel, you might sometimes want to pull up the full Google Contacts website for its complete set of features. Provided you’ve got Gmail’s keyboard shortcuts enabled now, commit this workaround to memory: Pressing g and then c will open up Contacts in a separate tab, no matter what else you’re doing in your inbox. Composing shortcuts Editor’s note: Assuming you’ve enabled keyboard shortcuts (see tip 3), the following keyboard shortcuts work in any browser on any desktop operating system. Mac users, just swap in the ⌘ key for “Ctrl” wherever you see it. 7. Ever like marking messages as unread after you’ve opened ’em? Gmail makes that incredibly easy to do: Anytime you have an email open, look for the envelope icon directly to the right of the trash can in the horizontal row of icons above your message (in the area directly beneath the search bar). That’ll let you mark the message as unread with a single click. Or, for a faster and more powerful one-two punch, just type an underscore ( _ ) while viewing any message. That’ll mark it as unread and zap you back to your main inbox. 8. Speaking of combining multiple actions into a single command, simplify your inbox organization process by enabling Gmail’s convenient Send & Archive button. It places a second button alongside the regular Send button whenever you’re responding to an existing message, and clicking that button (or, even better yet, hitting Ctrl-Enter on your keyboard) will send your response and archive the thread in one fell swoop. To enable it, look for the “Send and Archive” option within the General tab of Gmail’s settings. Click “Show ‘Send & Archive’ button in reply,” hit the Save Changes button at the bottom of the screen, and then get ready to save yourself steps the next time you type a reply. Gmail’s Send & Archive button (the blue one to the left of the regular Send button) turns two steps into one. JR Raphael / Foundry 9. I don’t know about you, but I frequently start typing an email and then decide against sending it. (Rather fittingly, I started typing out a lengthy explanation of the reasons but then decided against including it.) If the same thing ever happens to you, remember this: Hitting Ctrl-Shift-D while you’re in the Gmail compose tool will close the compose window and discard your draft. And it works whether you’re writing a new email or a reply. 10. Another awesome time-saver: In addition to the obvious Ctrl-B for bold and Ctrl-I for italics email formatting shortcuts, Gmail has hotkeys for doing some advanced forms of text formatting — things that’d otherwise require multiple clicks and much menu-hunting to accomplish. The ones I use the most: Ctrl-Shift-8 will add a bulleted list into your email (just like this list!), and Ctrl-Shift-7 will add a numbered one. Ctrl-Shift-9 will offset text in a blockquote style. Ctrl-] will indent text, while Ctrl-[ will remove any indentation. And Ctrl-\ will remove any formatting on your selected text and make it as plain as can be. 11. You’d never know it, but the Gmail compose tool itself can take on various forms, depending on your preferences. Make a mental note of these possibilities and the shortcuts to get to ’em: To start a new message in the default lower-right-corner-of-the-screen window view, hit c . To start a new message in a pop-up window totally separate from your main Gmail tab, hit Shift-C . You can do the same thing for a reply by hitting Shift-R while viewing a message thread — or Shift-A for reply-all. To start a new message in a full-screen compose window within your main Gmail tab, hit c — then click the little arrow icon in the compose tool’s upper-right corner. (You can also hit Shift while clicking that icon to pop the message out into a separate pop-up window form.) If you’d rather use that full-screen compose window all the time, by default, click the three-dot menu icon in the lower-right corner of the compose tool and look for the “Default to full-screen” option there. (If you ever change your mind, you’ll find the option to disable that preference in that very same spot.) If for some reason you like the idea of composing a message in a new tab instead of a pop-up window or within the main Gmail tab, just hit d while in your inbox. That’ll do the trick! To see more keyboard shortcuts, just type ? while viewing any message list within Gmail. Smarter snoozing 12. Don’t forget to take advantage of Gmail’s super-handy snoozing tool: Instead of letting messages linger in your inbox and pile up to an unmanageable point, use the snooze function to help yourself deal with everything as soon as you see it. A good rule of thumb to maintain: If you can respond to something in less than a minute, do it. If something doesn’t require any action on your behalf, archive it immediately. And if something requires some sort of action but you don’t have the time to mess with it at that moment, snooze it to a day and time when you will be able to handle it. You can snooze an email from your inbox by hovering over the message and selecting the clock-shaped Snooze icon, as noted in tip 2. You can also snooze an email while it’s open by clicking the three-dot menu icon to the right of the folder symbol directly above the email and then clicking “Snooze” within the menu that pops up. Or you can simply press b while you’re viewing a message or while you have it selected in your inbox. Snoozing a message causes it to vanish from your inbox and then reappear at any day and time you choose. JR Raphael / Foundry 13. Gmail even makes it possible to snooze multiple messages at the same time — in case you see more than one email that needs to be pushed back to the same point. From your inbox, simply click the boxes to the left of any messages you want to include, then click the three-dot menu icon within the row of icons toward the top of the screen and select “Snooze” from there. 14. Need to get back to something you snoozed — or change the day and time at which it’s set to reappear? You can always find all of your snoozed emails in Gmail’s Snoozed section, located beneath the “Inbox” line in the left-hand panel. Once you’re there, just hover over any email and click the clock-shaped icon to change its snooze settings or unsnooze it entirely. 15. You can snooze messages from the Gmail mobile apps, too, though the option is a bit buried. From the inbox view, press and hold a message to select it, then tap the three-dot menu icon at the top of the screen and look for “Snooze” in the list of options that appears. If you’ve already opened the message, tap the three-dot menu icon at the top of that screen; you should see “Snooze” show up as part of the options there as well. 16. Make snoozing even simpler in the Gmail mobile app by assigning it to one of your inbox swipe actions. Just open up the app, tap the three-line menu icon in its upper-left corner, then select “Settings.” On Android, tap “General settings” followed by “Swipe actions”; on iOS, you’ll tap “Inbox customizations” and then “Mail swipe actions.” All that’s left is to set either your left swipe or right swipe to “Snooze,” and then, you can simply swipe any message in that direction from your inbox to snooze it — no wasted taps or menu diving required. (The Gmail Android app has several other similarly useful hidden features , by the way, most of which aren’t available on iOS.) With one quick setting adjustment, you can snooze any message from the  Gmail mobile app simply by swiping it to the left or the right from your  inbox. JR Raphael / Foundry And with that, your Gmail time-saving toolbox is officially complete! The next logical step in your inbox improvement adventure is mastering the art of Gmail labels to fight back against email chaos — and I’ve got just the guide to get you started . This story was originally published in May 2018 and most recently updated in September 2026.

11. You’d never know it, but the Gmail compose tool itself can take on various forms, depending on your preferences. Make a mental note of these possibilities and the shortcuts to get to ’em:

  • To start a new message in the default lower-right-corner-of-the-screen window view, hit c.
  • To start a new message in a pop-up window totally separate from your main Gmail tab, hit Shift-C. You can do the same thing for a reply by hitting Shift-R while viewing a message thread — or Shift-A for reply-all.
  • To start a new message in a full-screen compose window within your main Gmail tab, hit c — then click the little arrow icon in the compose tool’s upper-right corner. (You can also hit Shift while clicking that icon to pop the message out into a separate pop-up window form.)
  • If you’d rather use that full-screen compose window all the time, by default, click the three-dot menu icon in the lower-right corner of the compose tool and look for the “Default to full-screen” option there. (If you ever change your mind, you’ll find the option to disable that preference in that very same spot.)
  • If for some reason you like the idea of composing a message in a new tab instead of a pop-up window or within the main Gmail tab, just hit d while in your inbox. That’ll do the trick!

To see more keyboard shortcuts, just type ? while viewing any message list within Gmail.

Smarter snoozing

12. Don’t forget to take advantage of Gmail’s super-handy snoozing tool: Instead of letting messages linger in your inbox and pile up to an unmanageable point, use the snooze function to help yourself deal with everything as soon as you see it.

A good rule of thumb to maintain: If you can respond to something in less than a minute, do it. If something doesn’t require any action on your behalf, archive it immediately. And if something requires some sort of action but you don’t have the time to mess with it at that moment, snooze it to a day and time when you will be able to handle it.

You can snooze an email from your inbox by hovering over the message and selecting the clock-shaped Snooze icon, as noted in tip 2. You can also snooze an email while it’s open by clicking the three-dot menu icon to the right of the folder symbol directly above the email and then clicking “Snooze” within the menu that pops up. Or you can simply press b while you’re viewing a message or while you have it selected in your inbox.

Snoozing a message causes it to vanish from your inbox and then reappear at any day and time you choose.

JR Raphael / Foundry

13. Gmail even makes it possible to snooze multiple messages at the same time — in case you see more than one email that needs to be pushed back to the same point. From your inbox, simply click the boxes to the left of any messages you want to include, then click the three-dot menu icon within the row of icons toward the top of the screen and select “Snooze” from there.

14. Need to get back to something you snoozed — or change the day and time at which it’s set to reappear? You can always find all of your snoozed emails in Gmail’s Snoozed section, located beneath the “Inbox” line in the left-hand panel. Once you’re there, just hover over any email and click the clock-shaped icon to change its snooze settings or unsnooze it entirely.

15. You can snooze messages from the Gmail mobile apps, too, though the option is a bit buried. From the inbox view, press and hold a message to select it, then tap the three-dot menu icon at the top of the screen and look for “Snooze” in the list of options that appears. If you’ve already opened the message, tap the three-dot menu icon at the top of that screen; you should see “Snooze” show up as part of the options there as well.

16. Make snoozing even simpler in the Gmail mobile app by assigning it to one of your inbox swipe actions. Just open up the app, tap the three-line menu icon in its upper-left corner, then select “Settings.” On Android, tap “General settings” followed by “Swipe actions”; on iOS, you’ll tap “Inbox customizations” and then “Mail swipe actions.”

All that’s left is to set either your left swipe or right swipe to “Snooze,” and then, you can simply swipe any message in that direction from your inbox to snooze it — no wasted taps or menu diving required. (The Gmail Android app has several other similarly useful hidden features, by the way, most of which aren’t available on iOS.)

With one quick setting adjustment, you can snooze any message from the  Gmail mobile app simply by swiping it to the left or the right from your  inbox.

JR Raphael / Foundry

And with that, your Gmail time-saving toolbox is officially complete! The next logical step in your inbox improvement adventure is mastering the art of Gmail labels to fight back against email chaos — and I’ve got just the guide to get you started.

items.title: This tech CEO said he wants the 'D+ version' of employee ideas. Read his AI writing memo.
items.summary: Spellbook CEO Scott Stevenson wants to see the "D+ version" of employees' ideas before they turn to AI. Alex Broadway/Web Summit via Sportsfile via Getty Images Spellbook's CEO says AI can make employees' ideas look more polished than their thinking. The AI company's new policy limits how workers can use AI to write project proposals. Stevenson would rather see a few rough bullets: "I want the D+ version of your plan." Scott Stevenson doesn't want every employee's idea to get an AI glow-up. The cofounder and CEO of Spellbook said workers' proposals containing "AI nonsense" routinely make it to his desk. It might be a project plan or a marketing pitch. Whatever it is, he said, it can arrive looking far more polished than the thinking behind it. Stevenson said he would rather see the rough version first. "I want the D+ version of your plan," he said. Stevenson is now asking employees at the Toronto company, which develops an AI tool for drafting and analyzing contracts, to resist the temptation to turn every idea into polished corporate prose. His message is a notable one coming from the CEO of an AI company : Use the technology, yet don't let it obscure your thinking . AI slop on social media and networking sites like LinkedIn has drawn plenty of attention. Stevenson is worried about a workplace version of the problem. Other companies are grappling with this challenge, too: The head of AI video company Synthesia warned staff earlier this year about " AI sloppification ," writing that overly wordy documents could mean that instead of one staffer taking 10 minutes to sharpen a document, "we have 10 people spending 10 additional minutes reading slop." Business Insider previously reported on AI software startup Clay's new companywide AI-writing policy . It focuses on four principles, including "writing is thinking" and "longer is not better." Stevenson is trying to tackle the problem with his own guidelines. He recently sent a memo to the company's 200-plus employees updating the company's AI policy and outlining how he wants them to use the technology. Here's an excerpt: While we are an AI company, and believe in the usefulness of AI, we think that today it works best in highly constrained work like coding or contract review. We do not believe that models are good at unconstrained longform writing, yet. Documents end up too long while saying too little, use repetitive language that decreases trust in your thinking, and sometimes contain ungrounded nonsense. While being able to create a polished longform document with a prompt may feel powerful and professional—this impression is often only surface level. Good writing is concise and authentic. I would rather that you send a scrappy 5 bullet point proposal than 5 pages of polished fluff. Furthermore, AI writing has become increasingly recognizable . We want our customers to always feel our care when we communicate with them, and we don't think that AI generated writing accomplishes this. Our new AI policy is as follows: You should indicate if a document or message you are sending internally was drafted with AI : this helps the reader digest it appropriately. AI should not be used for writing the main body of project proposals: we want to see your authentic reasoning. You may use AI for supplemental materials like spreadsheets and tables, but not for the core of your reasoning. a. When in doubt, send a "D+ Version": we often don't want a long or polished document. Concise authentic bullet points are often enough to get a conversation going. Thinking about how to make your argument succinct is helpful for the reader. Writing you send will be treated as your own: A lawyer is accountable if they submit an argument with hallucinated case law. We will also hold ourselves accountable for our own writing. Please review everything that you send to the team thoroughly, as it will be treated as your own Customer communications should always be hand-written: We want our 5,000 customers to feel authentic human care with every interaction. Is your company rethinking its policy on AI in the workplace? How do you feel about receiving writing produced with AI? Let us know in the comments below. items.title: I was sick of sending traditional applications. This is the email that finally got me hired.
items.summary: Judy Zeng sent a cold outreach email to a CEO and ended up getting a job as a result. Judy Zeng Judy Zeng sent a cold email to the CEO of EO studios. It resulted in an internship offer. She suggests doing research on LinkedIn to learn more about a CEO's philosophy before reaching out. Zeng said luck plays a role in success, and whether the company is open to non-traditional hiring. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Judy Zeng, a 22-year-old business development intern at global media startup EO Studios, based in San Francisco. Her identity and employment have been verified by Business Insider. This story has been edited for length and clarity. I'm a recent graduate from Northwestern University, where I studied journalism. I now work at a company called EO Studios. As a media major, there was always a lot of stress around finding internships and jobs. With all the AI applications and AI-powered reviewers, I had a lot of disillusionment with the traditional hiring process as a senior. I sent about 30 applications but never knew if they were being seen. I felt like I could keep applying to jobs all day and not get anything. In order to be more effective with my outreach , I figured I would try to be more strategic. Volume wasn't my strength. I tried an alternate method I produced a video story for a class assignment that was about how journalists turned their cold emails into cold outreach for jobs . One Northwestern alum who had the same double major as me said he cold emailed a YouTube personality , and now he's working as their head of content. A lot of the people I spoke to made me feel there was an alternative to the traditional hiring process , and I was inspired by that. I felt like there was something really audacious and daring about reaching out to someone directly for a job. I never felt like I was one of those people, but I knew I had initiative, so I was like, why not try this out? There was also an aspect of this strategy that felt like part of the job. As a journalism major, I took pride in being able to sleuth out emails and talk to the people I was interested in. I decided to try it out. This is the message I sent the CEO of the company I currently work for: Hi [recipient], I'm Judy Zeng, a senior at Northwestern University studying journalism and economics. I'm super passionate about tech and media, and in the past year, I founded a video production studio with 40K+ views and 50+ people featured on video. Here's my LinkedIn profile for reference. I've been following EO Studio's content and brand for a while now, and I think what you're doing is truly exceptional. I'd love to join the team and help grow your company. Here are a few specific ways I see myself adding value: Grow out EO's advertising and partnership infrastructure to increase revenue outside of YouTube monetization. Support the content production team by researching subjects, preparing questions, and interviewing subjects with my journalism background. Conduct quantitative research on what kinds of videos perform best on YouTube in order to inform what your next viral video looks like. Would you be open to a conversation one day in the coming weeks? I also saw that you're looking to expand your global presence in the United States and have moved your leadership meetings to English. I'd love to add a new perspective to your team as a native of Silicon Valley with connections in the Chicago area, where I'm currently located for school. Let me know what you think! Thanks, Judy This was the first time I tried something like this. The CEO didn't respond at first, so I sent a quick follow-up. He then thanked me for reaching out and said he was interested in speaking. After the reply, I had a conversation with a senior member he looped in. Then I was able to meet up with the CEO in San Francisco since I was visiting the Bay Area over spring break. In our conversation, we discussed the company, his vision, and the new media landscape. Both of my conversations with the senior member and CEO felt more like coffee chats than formal interviews. Afterward, I got a verbal offer. Understand the company before you reach out If you're used to sending out mass applications, this is a different framework where you want to think carefully about the company you want to join and whether it would be a good fit. You should take the time to really understand the company and its business needs first. I think using LinkedIn is an underrated strategy for understanding what's going on at certain companies and reaching them. A lot of CEOs, decision-makers, and senior-level folks post on LinkedIn about what's going on at the company, what they're thinking in the moment, and whether they're hiring. They post about their philosophies and if they're trying out new experiments. Luck plays a role I would definitely recommend reaching out to a CEO, but it depends on the content or the company you're reaching out to. This will not work out in every industry. I don't think you could email the CEO of a consulting giant and then get a job. It has to be a company that's OK with people disrupting traditional hierarchies or hiring pipelines. At the end of the day, a big part of success with this method is also luck. Did you get a job through cold outreach? We want to hear from you. I'm a recent graduate from Northwestern University, where I studied journalism. I now work at a company called EO Studios.

As a media major, there was always a lot of stress around finding internships and jobs. With all the AI applications and AI-powered reviewers, I had a lot of disillusionment with the traditional hiring process as a senior. I sent about 30 applications but never knew if they were being seen. I felt like I could keep applying to jobs all day and not get anything.

In order to be more effective with my outreach, I figured I would try to be more strategic. Volume wasn't my strength.

I tried an alternate method

I produced a video story for a class assignment that was about how journalists turned their cold emails into cold outreach for jobs. One Northwestern alum who had the same double major as me said he cold emailed a YouTube personality, and now he's working as their head of content.

A lot of the people I spoke to made me feel there was an alternative to the traditional hiring process, and I was inspired by that. I felt like there was something really audacious and daring about reaching out to someone directly for a job. I never felt like I was one of those people, but I knew I had initiative, so I was like, why not try this out?

There was also an aspect of this strategy that felt like part of the job. As a journalism major, I took pride in being able to sleuth out emails and talk to the people I was interested in.

I decided to try it out. This is the message I sent the CEO of the company I currently work for:

Hi [recipient],I'm Judy Zeng, a senior at Northwestern University studying journalism and economics. I'm super passionate about tech and media, and in the past year, I founded a video production studio with 40K+ views and 50+ people featured on video. Here's my LinkedIn profile for reference.I've been following EO Studio's content and brand for a while now, and I think what you're doing is truly exceptional. I'd love to join the team and help grow your company. Here are a few specific ways I see myself adding value:
  1. Grow out EO's advertising and partnership infrastructure to increase revenue outside of YouTube monetization.
  2. Support the content production team by researching subjects, preparing questions, and interviewing subjects with my journalism background.
  3. Conduct quantitative research on what kinds of videos perform best on YouTube in order to inform what your next viral video looks like.
Would you be open to a conversation one day in the coming weeks?I also saw that you're looking to expand your global presence in the United States and have moved your leadership meetings to English. I'd love to add a new perspective to your team as a native of Silicon Valley with connections in the Chicago area, where I'm currently located for school.Let me know what you think!Thanks,Judy

This was the first time I tried something like this. The CEO didn't respond at first, so I sent a quick follow-up. He then thanked me for reaching out and said he was interested in speaking. After the reply, I had a conversation with a senior member he looped in. Then I was able to meet up with the CEO in San Francisco since I was visiting the Bay Area over spring break.

In our conversation, we discussed the company, his vision, and the new media landscape. Both of my conversations with the senior member and CEO felt more like coffee chats than formal interviews. Afterward, I got a verbal offer.

Understand the company before you reach out

If you're used to sending out mass applications, this is a different framework where you want to think carefully about the company you want to join and whether it would be a good fit.

You should take the time to really understand the company and its business needs first. I think using LinkedIn is an underrated strategy for understanding what's going on at certain companies and reaching them.

A lot of CEOs, decision-makers, and senior-level folks post on LinkedIn about what's going on at the company, what they're thinking in the moment, and whether they're hiring. They post about their philosophies and if they're trying out new experiments.

Luck plays a role

I would definitely recommend reaching out to a CEO, but it depends on the content or the company you're reaching out to.

This will not work out in every industry. I don't think you could email the CEO of a consulting giant and then get a job. It has to be a company that's OK with people disrupting traditional hierarchies or hiring pipelines. At the end of the day, a big part of success with this method is also luck.

items.title: Most national retailers close on 2 holidays. Costco shuts down for 7.
items.summary: Costco's holiday closing dates are posted at the front entrance of a Costco warehouse. Dominick Reuter/Business Insider No Costco for you on Labor Day - the warehouse has long closed US stores on seven holidays each year. The retailer's former CFO Richard Galanti told Business Insider the cost was never a consideration. "We never looked at the math," he said. If there's one thing Americans love to do with their free time, it's shop. Retailers often treat their customers' days off as an occasion to run promotions or otherwise get a boost — but not so much at Costco. The wholesale club has a longstanding policy of closing US stores on seven holidays, spaced throughout the year. Costco still runs Labor Day sales, you just can't get the deals at the warehouse on Labor Day itself. "We feel it is important for our employees to enjoy these holidays with their families/friends," CEO Ron Vachris told Business Insider via email. "That is the reason we close on these days." Costco's decision to close for a week's worth of days each year contrasts with most national chains' holiday schedules, which typically close for Thanksgiving and Christmas . Home improvement retailer Lowe's also closes on a third day: Easter Sunday. In addition to being posted on giant metal signs at warehouse entrances, the list of days is enshrined in the Costco employee agreement, which is negotiated every few years between workers and leadership. Former CFO Richard Galanti told Business Insider the employee agreement is generally similar to the labor contract Costco has with employees at locations with Teamsters union representation. And while US warehouses do hundreds of thousands of dollars in sales every day, Galanti said the cost of shutting down was never a consideration during his tenure with the company. "We never looked at the math," he said. "If it's the right thing to do, we do it." At the same time, Costco has such strong loyalty among its members that a holiday's sales don't entirely disappear — they shift. "You may lose a little business that day, but you're gonna get most of it back the day before or after," Galanti said. Here are the holidays on which US Costco warehouses are closed: New Year's Day Easter Sunday Memorial Day Independence Day Labor Day Thanksgiving Day Christmas Day Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: AI in cardiology: The path to practical application carries risks
items.summary: Dr Hannah van Kolfschooten (Photo: zVg) . By Yvonne Vahlensieck A new EU strategy is placing greater emphasis on artificial intelligence in the management of heart disease. Legal researcher Hannah van Kolfschooten believes this is premature. Among other things, she criticizes the fact that no concrete benefit for patients has yet been demonstrated and that there are gaps in the legislation. Dr van Kolfschooten, the EU presented its Safe Hearts Plan at the end of last year. It aims to help member states develop new strategies in the fight against cardiovascular disease. What role does artificial intelligence (AI) play here? AI plays a key role in this plan. It is to be used extensively in all three areas on which the fight against cardiovascular disease is based: prevention, early detection and screening, as well as treatment and care. In your article recently published in the scientific journal “Lancet Regional Health – Europe”, you criticize this focus on AI. In your view, there is a benefits gap. What do you mean by that? There is a great deal of research into AI in the field of healthcare. Under controlled conditions in a research environment, AI performs very well in all three areas mentioned above. These are promising approaches. But a positive study result is by no means a guarantee that things will go just as well in clinical practice and that people’s heart health will actually improve. Technically, AI may work very well, but healthcare systems are complex. Many practical, organisational, and legal barriers can prevent AI from delivering real benefits to patients. I therefore consider comprehensive implementation of AI in the field of cardiovascular disease to be premature. Could you give an example of such a benefit gap? An AI model may be able to accurately identify which people are at high risk of heart disease before any symptoms appear. However, a good AI prediction alone is not enough. Because it is not a given that this person will actually receive the appropriate care. Medical professionals also need to know what to do with such a prediction. In order to achieve this, there need to be defined processes in the healthcare system. The proper use of AI needs to become part of medical training. Even if we have a perfect prognosis, that does not mean that it will bring about any change in the health of individuals or in the healthcare system. You also point out that minorities are not sufficiently represented in AI models. Why is that? The data used to train AIs comes primarily from patient groups in which minorities are not represented. The gender balance isn’t representative either. When it comes to cardiovascular disease, there is less data available on women, even though they account for half of those affected. This inequality will continue to grow, as AI systems are expensive to implement. Consequently, they are unable to properly explain the reason for the planned procedure and the possible risks to the patient. You also see gaps in the legislation. However, AI gives rise to many gray areas when it comes to patients’ rights. For example, wearables such as smart watches collect health data and it is often unclear whether this data will be shared with third parties. Some wearables also provide information on a person’s state of health based on AI analyses. Her research focuses on the intersection between law, artificial intelligence and health. She is an expert member of AI committees at the World Health Organization and the EU.
items.summary_html:
Dr Hannah van Kolfschooten (Photo: zVg).

By Yvonne Vahlensieck

A new EU strategy is placing greater emphasis on artificial intelligence in the management of heart disease. Legal researcher Hannah van Kolfschooten believes this is premature. Among other things, she criticizes the fact that no concrete benefit for patients has yet been demonstrated and that there are gaps in the legislation.

Dr van Kolfschooten, the EU presented its Safe Hearts Plan at the end of last year. It aims to help member states develop new strategies in the fight against cardiovascular disease. What role does artificial intelligence (AI) play here?

AI plays a key role in this plan. It is to be used extensively in all three areas on which the fight against cardiovascular disease is based: prevention, early detection and screening, as well as treatment and care.

In your article recently published in the scientific journal “Lancet Regional Health – Europe”, you criticize this focus on AI. In your view, there is a benefits gap. What do you mean by that?

There is a great deal of research into AI in the field of healthcare. Under controlled conditions in a research environment, AI performs very well in all three areas mentioned above. These are promising approaches.

But a positive study result is by no means a guarantee that things will go just as well in clinical practice and that people’s heart health will actually improve. Technically, AI may work very well, but healthcare systems are complex. Many practical, organisational, and legal barriers can prevent AI from delivering real benefits to patients. I therefore consider comprehensive implementation of AI in the field of cardiovascular disease to be premature.

Could you give an example of such a benefit gap?

An AI model may be able to accurately identify which people are at high risk of heart disease before any symptoms appear. However, a good AI prediction alone is not enough. Because it is not a given that this person will actually receive the appropriate care. Medical professionals also need to know what to do with such a prediction. In order to achieve this, there need to be defined processes in the healthcare system. The proper use of AI needs to become part of medical training. Even if we have a perfect prognosis, that does not mean that it will bring about any change in the health of individuals or in the healthcare system.

You also point out that minorities are not sufficiently represented in AI models. Why is that?

The data used to train AIs comes primarily from patient groups in which minorities are not represented. The gender balance isn’t representative either.

When it comes to cardiovascular disease, there is less data available on women, even though they account for half of those affected. This inequality will continue to grow, as AI systems are expensive to implement. This means that only wealthy hospitals can afford them, and newly collected datasets will come primarily from affluent patients. This leads to a bias.

What risks are there for me as a patient as a result of the increased use of AI systems?

Autonomy is a top priority in our healthcare system. This means that patients should be fully informed before they consent to treatment. However, even doctors do not always understand how AI arrives at a specific recommendation. Consequently, they are unable to properly explain the reason for the planned procedure and the possible risks to the patient.

You also see gaps in the legislation. What problems might AI present us with in this regard?

In fact, everything in the healthcare sector is strictly regulated by law. For example, if a doctor is involved, they bear the responsibility. However, AI gives rise to many gray areas when it comes to patients’ rights.

For example, wearables such as smart watches collect health data and it is often unclear whether this data will be shared with third parties. Some wearables also provide information on a person’s state of health based on AI analyses. But who is liable if someone mistakenly believes they are healthy on the basis of such an analysis and does not go to hospital?

The Safe Hearts Plan is aimed at EU member states. What is the situation in Switzerland?

Switzerland is not required to follow these EU guidelines. However, it’s basically in the same situation when it comes to the use of AI. For example, University Hospital Basel is currently developing a number of AI applications. But even here in Switzerland, the transition from the research phase to real-world implementation is difficult.

But there’s no turning back now. AI will play an increasingly significant role in the field of heart health and other areas of medicine. What should we do?

Legislation always lags behind social development. That is why it is really important that we establish the legal framework for the use of AI now. But this alone is not enough. We also need to invest in medical training so that trainee doctors can acquire the necessary skills. And when it comes to AI applications, we should not only measure their technical performance, but also their clinical benefits. We need to tackle all of this immediately and simultaneously.
